caseno: Appeal from Appellate Decree No.708 of 1970.
lawyer:
Abdul Wadud Chowdhury ------ For the Appellant.  
T.H. Khan with M.A, Rouf and A.M. Jalaluddin ------ For the Respondents.
parties:
Jinnat Ali Muktear ------ Appellant.
Vs.
Abdul Majid ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
This appeal arises out of a suit for declaration that the plaintiff is entitled to get possession of the suit land.

2. The facts leading to this appeal in, brief are that the suit plots were recorded in the name of Peary Mohan Chakraborty and after his death it was owned and possessed by his son, Kanak Lal Chakraborty. It was the plaintiff's case that the suit land was exchanged by Kanak Lal Chakraborty with the land of Maharam Ali in Tripura State. The recorded owners executed a general Power of Attorney in favour of the plaintiff who was the uncle-in-law of the said Maharam Ali. It was further asserted that the plaintiff was in possession of the suit land as a Bargadar of the said Maharam Ali. The defendant was threatening the plaintiff with dispossession on the basis of a fraudulent deed of exchange and with that and in view he also initiated a proceeding under section 145 Cr.P.C. and the suit land was attached and the Officer-in-charge of Kotwali P.S. was appointed as the Receiver. Thereafter the said proceeding under section 145 Cr.P.C. was dropped but the land was kept under attachment and the parties were directed to seek relief in the Civil Court. Hence the present suit by the plaintiff.

3. The defendant contested the suit by filing a written statement wherein he denied the material allegations made in the plaint. His case was that the recorded owner Peary Mohan Chakraborty sold the suit land to his nephew, Profulla Kumar Chakraborty 17/18 years ago and delivered possession to Profulla. The defendant exchanged his land in Tripura State with the land of Profulla by a deed of exchange and since then he has been in possession.

4. Both sides adduced oral and documentary evidence in support of their respective cases. The learned Munsif upon a consideration of the evidence on record dismissed the suit holding that the suit was not maintainable without any prayer for declaration of the plaintiff's title and that the defendant was in possession of the suit land at the time of attachment. On appeal, The learned Subordinate Judge reversed the findings of the learned Munsif and allowed the appeal. Hence the present appeal at the instance of the defendant.

5. Mr. Abdul Wadud Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant has submitted firstly, that the suit itself was not maintainable without a prayer for declaration of title and it is hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act ; secondly, he has assailed the admissibility of a certified copy, Exhibit 5(a) under section 33 of the Evidence Act, and lastly, that it was not a proper judgment of reversal.

6. Mr. T. H. Khan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-respondent has replied to the various contentions raised on behalf of the appellant and has asserted that the suit was quite maintainable.

7. With regard to the first contention of the learned Advocate on the maintainability of the suit, it appears that the learned Munsif found that a suit for declaration of right to possession was not maintainable without a prayer for declaration of title. The learned Subordinate Judge has however reversed the Ending and has held that the suit was maintainable. Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act runs as follows :

Sec. 42 : —"Any person entitled to any legal character, or to any right as to any property, may institute a suit against any person denying, or interested to deny, his title to such character or right, and the court may in its discretion make therein a declaration that he is so entitled and the plaintiff need not in such suit ask for any further relief :

Bar to such declaration—Provided that no court shall make any such declaration where the plaintiff being able to seek further relief than a mere declaration of title, omits to do so."

<u>8. From a perusal of the section it is clear that not only a person entitled to any legal character but also any person entitled to any right as to any property can institute a suit for declaration. In this case it has been found by the learned Subordinate Judge that both the parties are without any title and the suit is for possessory right only. Possessory right is also certainly an enforceable right and it does not therefore, stand to any reason as to why a person cannot claim possessory right as against another person who also does not claim any title of his own. It is an established and well-settled principle of law that even a trespasser is entitled to maintain his possession against the entire world except the true owner. In the view that I have taken I am supported by a decision of the Privy Council in the case of Ismail Ariff Vs. Mohammad Ghouse. in 30 I.A. at page 99. In this case there was a suit for declaration of title and for injunction, the defence was that the land was subject to Wakf and the defendant was the Mutwalli thereof. Both the courts found that the plaintiff was in possession of the suit property and that the defendant was neither the Mutwalli nor he had any right, title in the suit property. The learned Single Judge of the High Court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiff has at least a title subject to the Wakf. On appeal, the Chief Justice and two other learned Judges who constituted the appellate Bench while agreeing with finding of possession in favour of the plaintiff, held that the plaintiff has required no title since his vendors had no right to alienate the suit property which was dedicated. Accordingly, the appeal was allowed and the suit was dismissed. On appeal by the plaintiffs, their Lordships of the Privy Council held that the plaintiff was entitled to a declaration as against the defendant who was without any title, that he was lawfully entitled to possession and the relief consequent thereon. Accordingly, the Privy Council reversed the decree of the appellate court and affirmed the decree passed by the learned Single Judge modifying the declaration by substituting the words that "plaintiff "the plaintiff is lawfully entitled to possession" for the words that "the plaintiff is the sole and absolute owner. Nearer home, I find that in the case of Ramalinga Pamdaram and others Vs. Anthenimuthu Vathiar and others, in A.I.R. 1934 Madras at page 274. it was held that where the only question is the possession of the plaintiff as against the defendant no question as to who is the real owner of the land arises and the plaintiff is entitled to a declaration that he is lawfully entitled to the possession of the land. In the case of Aminul Islam Vs. M/s. Kilburn & Co. Ltd., in 18 D.L.R. at page 691, it has been held that if a person takes possession of a property which belongs to another he does not become the owner but his possession is good as against another except the true owner and if the possessory owner is wrongly deprived of his possession by a person other than the true owner he can recover it.</u>

<u>9. I am in respectful agreement with the principles laid down by their lordships in the above mentioned cases and it is therefore clear that a possessory owner is also entitled to maintain his possession, be he a bargadar or even a trespasser as against the entire world except in the rightful owner. Here in the instant case, the plaintiff is in possession of the suit land as a bargadar as well as by virtue of a power of attorney executed by the recorded owner. The plaintiff does not claim any title for himself. All that he claims is the possessory right or possessory ownership in the suit land. I am therefore, of the opinion that the suit at the instance of the plaintiff is quite maintainable and is not hit by Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The suit land is admittedly under attachment and is now under the custody of the court through a Receiver appointed by the court and as such the question of recovery of possession does not arise. In this view of the matter the only prayer that the plaintiff could validly make was a prayer for declaration of his right to possession of the land free of attachment and this having been done, I find that the suit was quite maintainable. This view of mine finds support from a decision of a Division Bench in the case of K. Sandarasa Iyer Vs. Sarvajana Soirklabi Vindhl Nidhi Ltd., reported in A.I.R. 1939 (Madras) at Page 853. The contention of the learned Advocate is, therefore, without any substance;</u>

<u>10. With regard to the next submission of the learned Advocate for the appellant that the certified copy, Exhibit 5(a) was inadmissible in view of Section 33 of the Evidence Act, I am unable to appreciate the logic of the argument advanced by the learned Advocate. This objection appears to have been taken for the first time in appeal before the learned Sub-ordinate Judge who has elaborately dealt with the point and negatived the objection. The learned Subordinate Judge in support of his finding has relied on a decision of the Privy Council reported in A.I.R. 1943 (P.C.) at page 83. This case I find was relied upon and followed by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the case of Abdullah and others Vs. Abdul Karim and others, in 20 DL.R. (S.C.) at page 205 wherein it was held that it was now well settled that if objection to the formal proof of a document has not been taken at the earliest point of time it cannot be taken subsequently and certainly not in appeal. I am, therefore, inclined to agree with the learned Subordinate Judge that the certified copy was legally admitted The contention of the learned Advocate in this regard is also without any force.</u>

11. Lastly, the learned Advocate for the appellant has argued that it was not a proper judgment of reversal. I have gone through the judgment of both the courts below and I find that the learned Subordinate Judge has adverted to the findings of the learned Munsif and has reversed the same after proper appreciation of the evidence on record with his own reasoning’s which I find quite cogent and satisfactory. No illegality or irregularity could be pointed out by the learned Advocate in the said findings.

12. The learned Subordinate Judge has found that there were interpolations in Exhibit A, the sole basis of the defendant's claim of possession and has disbelieved the same. He was further found that there was no documentary evidence to show that Piyari Mohan, the original owner ever sold the suit land to Prafulla from whom the defendant obtained the alleged deed of exchange. Moreover, the record of rights stands in the name of Piyari Mohan and the plaintiff claims possession through the son of Piyari Mohan. In the proceeding u/s 145 Cr. P. C., the defendant's sole witness, Sikandar Ali admitted the possession of the plaintiff in the suit land and certified copy of the deposition of the said witness has been marked as exhibit 5(a) in the suit. Having regard to these facts and circumstances, I am inclined to agree with the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge that the plaintiff and not the defendant was in possession of the suit land prior to the attachment. The grievance of the  learned Advocate in this regard also fails. No other ground has been urged. For the reasons stated above, I find no substance in the appeal which is accordingly dismissed with costs.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 586 of 1997.
lawyer:
Md Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ------- For the Petitioners. 
Not represented ------- The Respondent.
parties:
Abdur Rashid (Md) and others ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Bainchitala Junior High School ----- Respondent
case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated 2nd March, 1997 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1751 of 1995).
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J : This petition for leave to appeal has been preferred against the judgment and order dated 2nd March, 1997 of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1751 of 1995 discharging the Rule which was obtained against the order No. 15 dated 22nd February, 1995 of the learned District Judge, Jhenaidha in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 54 of 1985 allowing an application under Order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure (CPC) and thereby adding one Khandker Moulana Meshbahul Alam Azad Khandani as appellant in the miscellaneous appeal pending before the Court of District Judge.

2. Facts, in short, are that petitioner herein filed Title Suit No. 16 of 1981 (previously numbered as Title Suit No. 26 of 1979 of the Court of Subordinate Judge, Jessore) of the Court of Subordinate Judge, Jhenidha seeking declaration that he is the successor of the defendant Bainchitala Islamia Junior Madrasah and for a further declaration of title to the land described in the schedule appended to the plaint. The suit was decreed ex parte on 20th November, 1982. Defendant Nos. 6 and 7 (Badaruddin Mandal) of the aforementioned suit filed an application under Order IX rule 13 CPC for setting aside of the ex parte decree and thereupon Miscellaneous Case No. 76 of 1982 was registered. The said miscellaneous case was ultimately dismissed on 23rd April 1985. As against the order of dismissal defendant No. 7 preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 54 of 1985 before the Court of District Judge and therein one Khandker Moulana Meshbahul Alam Azad Khandani filed an application under Order I rule 10 CPC claiming himself as Secretary of the Madrasah for being added as appellant in the miscellaneous appeal and the said application was allowed and as against that Revisional application was moved and Rule was obtained, Civil Revision No. 216/85(Jessore)/3602/91 (Dhaka) and finally, the Rule was made absolute on 2nd August, 1994. It may be mentioned during the pendency of the civil revision defendant No. 7 Badaruddin Mandai who was the appellant in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 54 of 1985 died on 22nd December, 1992. That on receipt of the record from the High Court Division the same was shown to the learned Advocate of the defendant-appellant on 8th January, 1995 and an application under Order I rule 10 read with section 151 of the CPC was filed on 22nd February, 1995 seeking addition of the heirs of Badaruddin MandaI as appellants in the Miscellaneous Appeal No. 54 of 1985 and the said application was allowed on 22nd February, 1995. As against the said order plaintiff-respondent in the miscellaneous case moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction and obtained the present Rule contending that as no estate has been left by Badaruddin to which the petitioners can be considered to have succeeded on his death and consequently, they do not come within the ambit of legal representative as contemplated by the provision of Rule 4 of Order XXII of the CPC.

3. It may be mentioned that defendant No.7 Badaruddin in his application under Order IX rule 13 of the CPC stated that he was entrusted by the Madrasah to manage its property. It was also stated in the application under Order I rule 10 that Badaruddin was a bargader of the land in suit under the Madrasah and that after death of their father petitioners have taken barga of the land in suit from the Madrasah.

<u>4. In the background of the aforesaid facts the High Court Division upon observing even if the facts as stated by the petitioners in assertion of their right to be added as parties (appellants) in the appeal were taken to be correct "then also they cannot be added as parties in the instant suit because they have no independent right to call in question the legality and propriety of the decree passed in Title Suit No. 16 of 1981 wherein they were not parties".</u>

5. "Be it an application under Order I rule 10 of the Code or an application for substitution under Order XXII rule 4 of the Code, the opposite parties must show that they have inherited the estate left by their deceased father, but it is clear from the assertion made by both deceased Badaruddin in his application under Order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the present opposite parties in their application under Order I rule 10 of the Code that no estate has been left by their father to which they have succeeded on his death. Thus, they do not come within the ambit of legal representative as contemplated in rule 4 of Order XXII of the Code."

6. In the instant case admittedly the suit property is not the personal property of deceased Badaruddin and it did never belong to him. So, no question of inheritance does arise in respect of the suit land by the opposite parties as heirs of deceased Badaruddin. In that view of the matter the application filed by them can neither be allowed under Order I rule 10 or under Order XXII, rule 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the learned appellate Court below, misdirecting himself on a total misconception of law and facts erroneously allowed the application filed by the opposite parties for adding them as appellants in the Miscellaneous Appeal No. 54 of 1985 made the Rule absolute.

7. As against the order of the High Court Division dated 12nd March, 1997 making the Rule absolute and thereby rejecting the present petitioners application under Order I rule 10 read with section 151 CPC for being added as appellants in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 54 of 1985 of the court of District Judge, Jhenidah this leave petition has been filed.

8. Mr Md Aftab Hossain, learned Advocate-on-Record for the petitioners, submits that Badaruddin, predecessor of the petitioners, as was impleded in suit and that on the death of Badaruddin as the petitioners are the bargader of the land in suit and in the background of the aforesaid facts the petitioners were being the necessary and proper parties in the suit as well as in the miscellaneous appeal the High Court Division was in error in rejecting the petitioners' application filed under Order J rule 10 read with section 151 CPC.

9. It is seen from the judgment of the High Court Division that Badaruddin in his application filed under Order IX rule 13 stated that Madrasah entrusted the management of the property in suit to him but Badaruddiu's heirs, petitioners herein, in their application under Order I rule 10 read with section 151 CPC in support of their claim of being added as appellant in the miscellaneous appeal stated that their father was a bargader of the land in suit and that after him they are the bargaders in the land in suit.

10. In the background of the facts stated by petitioner's father in the petition filed under Order IX rule 13 CPC and the petitioners herein in their petition filed under Order I rule 10 read with section 151 CPC the High Court Division arrived at the finding "that no Estate has been left by their father to which they have succeeded on his death. Thus they do not come within the ambit of legal representative as contemplated in rule 4 or Order XXII of the Code."

In the light of the undisputed facts of the instant case we are of the view that there is no infirmity in the finding made by the High Court Division as to petitioners not being legal representative of defendant No. 7 in respect of the subject matter of the suit. The learned Advocate-on-Record for the petitioners could not point out any error or infirmity in the judgment of the High Court Division in any respect.

Accordingly, the petition is dismissed.

End.

caseno: Civil Revision No. 4639 of 1995 with Civil Revision No. 4640 of 1995.
lawyer:
Mahmudul Islam, Advocate ----- For the Petitioners 
MI Faruqui with M Saleemullah, Advocates  ----- For the Opposite Party
parties:
Mohammadullah and others ----- Petitioners 
Vs.
Md Shamsul Alam alias Md  Alam   ----- Opposite Party
full_judgment:
Abdul Wahhab Miah, J: These two Rules have arisen out of two orders of similar nature passed in Miscellaneous Case Nos. 29 of 1995 and 30 of 1995 both dated 31-10-1995 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka allowing the said cases which were filed under Order IX rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. As similar facts and question of law are involved these Rules have been heard together and are disposed of by this single judgment.

2. The petitioners in both the Rules as plaintiffs filed Title Suit Nos. 172 of 1991 and 173 of 1991 in the court of Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka on the same day for eviction of their monthly tenants, namely, Md Shamsul Alam @ Md Alam and Haji Abdul Jabbar respectively from the suit premises. Both the suits were decreed ex parte on 26-2-1992. The decrees were put into execution vide Title Execution Case Nos. 8 of 1992 and 9 of 1992 of the same Court and in execution of the said decrees the defendants of both the suits were evicted from the respective suit premises. Thereafter, two separate applications were filed by the said two respective defendant, under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte decree stating, inter alia, that summons of the suits were not served upon them and the plaintiffs in collusion with the process server showed the summons served by hanging and managed to have the ex parte decree. The defendant-petitioners came to know about the respective ex parte decree on 14-1-1995, and then the police evicted them from their respective suit premises On such knowledge the petitioners through their learned Advocate enquired into the matter in court and came to know definitely about the ex parte decree. The said applications were registered as Miscellaneous Case Nos. 3 of 1995 and 4 of 1995. Eventually, both the said miscellaneous cases were transferred to the court of Assistant Judge, 4th Court. Dhaka and were renumbered as Miscellaneous Case Nos. 29 of 1995 and 38 of 1995.

3. The Miscellaneous cases were contested by the plaintiffs by filing separate written objection stating, inter alia, that the summons of the suits was duly served upon the respective defendant. The process server went to the suit premises to serve the summons of the respective suit, but since the defendant refused to accept the summons the process server served the same by hanging. Besides, the service of summons by hanging the same was also served by registered post as the postal peon returned the same with the endorsement 'refused'. As the defendant of the respective suits did not contest the suit the court below rightly decreed the same ex parte.

4. At the time of hearing of the cases each of the defendant-petitioners examined 3 witnesses; on the other hand, the plaintiff-opposite parties examined 2 witnesses including the process server. The court below on consideration of the evidence on record, both oral and documentary, disbelieved the testimony of the process server and came to the definite finding that the report of the process server could not be believed as there was overwriting on the service of summons, and that although the suit was filed on 13-11-1991, yet the process server served the summons on 19-9-1991. The court below also found that there was no address of the attesting witnesses as well as their signature on the service return which were shown to have been served by hanging. The court below on the positive finding that summons of the suit was not served upon the respective defendants of the suits and that the defendants had no knowledge about the ex parte decree allowed both the miscellaneous cases and set aside the ex parte decree and restored the suit to its file and number.

5. Mr. Mahmudul Islam, learned Advocate appearing in both the Rules for the petitioners, submits that the court below was in error in holding that since the service of summons by the process server was not proved, it did not matter whether summons of the suit was served by registered post. He submits with reference to rule 19B (2) of the Code of Civil Procedure (hereinafter referred to as the Code) that summons of the suit was served upon both the defendants of the suits by registered post and the postal peon returned the postal articles containing the summons with the endorsement 'refused', The court below committed error of law in setting the ex parte decree passed in both the suits and, as such, the impugned orders are liable to be set aside.

6. Mr MI Faruqui, learned Advocate appearing for the defendant-opposite party in both the Rules, on the other hand, submits that the postal article, namely, the envelope, the summons and acknowledgment due, which were allegedly sent to the address of the respective defendants of both the suits, but returned by the postal peon with the endorsement 'refused' do not show that copy of the plaint accompanied the summons. Mr Paruqui submits that in order to constitute summons within the meaning of Order IV, rule 1 (b) of the Code, copy of the plaint must be accompanied with the summons. And if the summons sent to the defendant did not accompany the plaint even if the same was returned by the postal peon with the endorsement 'refused' that would not be a refusal by the defendant within the Meaning of Order V, sub-rule 2, of Rule 19B of the Code and such refusal could not be accepted as a proper service of summons of the suit upon the defendant by registered post to hear the suit ex parte, the court below rightly set aside the ex parte decrees.

7. Mr Faruqui drew my attention to the fact that the envelopes which were allegedly sent to the respective defendants of the suits for service of summons by registered post are with the record and contain only the summons. I have seen the envelope. I have found only the summons and no copy of the plaint accompanying it.

<u>8. Order IV of the Code has dealt with the procedure of institution of suit and Order V of the Code has dealt with issue and service of summons. In answer to point raised by the learned Advocate, I feel it necessary to quote the relevant rules of the two Orders of the Code, namely, rule (1b) of Order IV and rule 2 of Order V. Rule (1b) is as under.</u>

<u>"a plaintiff shall file, along with the plaint, for each defendant a copy of the summons along with a pre-paid registered acknowledgment due cover with complete and correct address of the defendant written on it."</u>

<u>Rule 2 of Order V of the Code is as under:</u>

<u>"Every summon shall be accompanied by a copy of the plaint or, if so permitted, by a concise statement".</u>

<u>From a reading of the above two provisions to me that copy of the plaint is an integral part of the summons. In other words, to constitute a summons, within the meaning of the said provisions of the Code plaint must be accompanied with the summons either it be served by the process server or by registered post.</u>

9. As found hereinbefore the summons of the respective suits which were returned by the postal peon with the endorsement 'refused' did not accompany the plaint. And, as such, refusal to receive the summons, if there be any, by the respective defendants of the suits could be construed as refusal within the meaning of rule 19B(2) of Order V of the Code so as to accept the same as proper service of summons by registered post and then hear the suit ex parte. For the discussions made above, I find substance in the submission of Mr MI Faruqui and hold that the summons in both suits were not at all served upon the respective defendants by registered post. So far as the findings of the courts below as regard the service of summons by the process server. Mr Islam found it difficult to assail the same with reference to the materials on record. Since the trial Court on consideration of the evidence on record, both oral and documentary, came to the definite finding that the summons of the suit was not served upon the respective defendants of both the suits and that the respective defendant had no knowledge about the suit and the ex parte decree till 14-1-1995 which are based on proper consideration of the evidence on record this court sitting in revision cannot interfere with the said finding of fact.

In the result these Rules are discharged without any order as to cost. The impugned orders are maintained.

End.

caseno: Writ Petition No. 3127 of 1997 with petition No. 3128 of 1997.
lawyer:
Fariduddin Ahmed with Md Kamrul Islam, Advocates ------ For the Petitioner. (In both the Writ Petitions) 
Adilur Rahman Deputy Attorney-General with Md Zafor Imam, Assistant Attorney-General, Shamsul Hoque and Quamrun Nessa Ratna, Advocates------ For Respondent No.2. 
AY Masihuzzaman, Advocate------ For Respondent No. 1 in Writ Petition No.3127 of 1997.
parties:
Ali Ashraf Mia ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Chairman, First Court of Settlement and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Tariq-ul-Hakim J : . Rules Nisi were issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and orders dated 13-2-1996 and 12-11-1995 vide Annexure-B of the Writ Petition passed by the respondent No. 1, First Court of Settlement in Case No. 20 of 1990 (Ka-44 Block- B, Babar Road, Dhaka) and Case No. 65 of 1990 (Ka 45 Block B Mohammadpur, Dhaka) should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and are of no legal effect and why the properties in question should not be excluded from the list of Abandoned Property published in the official gazette dated 23-9-1986 and/or pass such other or further order of orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Both the Rules have been issued at the instance of the petitioner and concern similar facts and point of law and, as such, are being disposed of by this single judgment.

3. In Writ Petition No. 3127 of 1997 it has been stated that the property at No. 16/13, Block-B, Babar Road, Mohammadpur, Dhaka belonged to one Fouzdar Miah who entered into an agreement on 5-3-1973 for sale of the said property to the petitioner and subsequently, since the said owner did not execute and register the sale deed in favour of the petitioner, he was constrained to institute Title Suit No. 1110 of 1991 in the 4th Court of the Subordinate Judge, Dhaka for specific performance of contract. The said suit was ultimately decreed ex parte on 15-8-1983 and a sale deed was executed and registered through the court on 17-11-1983. The petitioner further contends that he was given possession of the said house through the court on 12-1-1984 and the Government allegedly excluded the said house property from the list of abandoned properties and intimated the same to the petitioner vide Memo No. Section 9/A-73/83/1157 dated 28-12-1983 (Annexure-A). It is further stated that though the Government had filed Miscellaneous Case No. 31 of 1985 under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte decree, the case was dismissed on contest by the judgment and order dated 31-3-1986. Appeal was filed to the learned District Judge, Dhaka and thereafter to the High Court Division and lastly, to the Appellate Division but ultimately the aforesaid ex parte decree was not set aside. In the meantime, the aforesaid property was included in the Ka list of the Abandoned Buildings as published in the official Gazette on 23-9-1986 and the petitioner filed Case No. 20 of 1990 in the First Court of Settlement under section 7(1) of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 for exclusion of the property from the said list. The Government contested the case alleging, inter alia, that the said property was leased out to one Fouzdar Miah, a refugee, for his rehabilitation and thereafter, since 1972, the property became an abandoned property and different persons were given lease of the said house by the government who have been occupying the same. The First Court of Settlement by its judgment and order dated 13-2-1996 dismissed the petitioner's case and refused to exclude the house from the Ka list of Abandoned Buildings.

4. Being aggrieved, the petitioner has come to this Court and obtained the present Rules.

5. The respondent No.2 the Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Housing and Public Works, is contesting the Rules by filing Affidavit-in-Opposition where it is stated, inter alia, that the suit property at No. 16/13, Block-B, Babar Road, Mohammadpur, Dhaka was leased out to one Fouzdar Miah, a Non Bengali and his whereabouts were not known after the War of Independence in 1971 and, as such, the property vested with the Government as an Abandoned Property under President's Order 16 of 1972 and was included in the Ka list of abandoned properties published in the Bangladesh Gazette dated 23-9-1986. It has been further stated that the suit property was under control, management and supervision of the Government through different allottees since 1972 onward till today. It has been further stated that the petitioner obtained an ex parte decree from the court on 15-8-1983 by suppressing material facts in respect of the said property and by practising fraud upon the court and also thereafter managed to have a deed of sale executed and registered through court on 20-11-1983 on the basis of the aforesaid fraudulent decree. It has been further stated that the petitioner never got possession of the suit property through court on 12-1-1984 as alleged. It has been further stated that the Government never excluded the said property from the Ka list of abandoned property and the question of intimating the same to the petitioner vide Memo No. Section 9/A-73/83/1157 dated 28-12-1983 (Annexure-A) as alleged by the petitioner does not arise. It has also been stated that no such letter was issued from the Ministry of Housing and Public Works or its Department in favour of the petitioner. It has been further stated that the said Fouzdar Miah left this country during the liberation war and that he has not been found any where in Bangladesh. Thereafter, one Abu Saved was found in the suit property and the Government issued DN in his favour in 1975 and he paid rent to the Government from 1972. Subsequently, however, he rented the said allotted house to other persons permanently as a result of which his allotment by the Government was cancelled and the same was alloted to one Rehana Parvin vide Memo No. DA, AO-199/79-451/14 dated 25-6-1979, a Government employee of Family Planning Department and she has been paying rent regularly to the Government and that she has been residing in the said property till date. It has been further stated that the petitioner has made false and fabricated papers to support his claim on the property and, as such, the impugned order of the First Court of Settlement calls for no interference by this Court.

6. This Rule is also being contested by one Rehana Parvin, added respondent No. 3, who has filed separate Affidavit-in-Opposition denying the material allegation in the Writ Petition. It has been stated therein that the original owner of the property was the Government of East Pakistan who leased it out to one Fauzdar Miah and the said Fouzdar Miah having left the house abandoned during the liberation war in 1971, the Government of Bangladesh took possession and control of the same in accordance with law and allotted it to one Abu Sayed who, in violation of the lease agreement, rented it out to other persons. Subsequently, the Government cancelled the allotment of the said Abu Sayed and took possession of the house in question and in 1979 allotted the same to the respondent No. 3 vide Memo No. DA, AO-199/78-451/14 and handed over possession of the same to her on 29-5-1979. The said respondent No. 3 has been continuously possessing the said house since then. It has been further stated that the Government challenging the ex parte decree dated 15-8-1983 passed in Title Suit No. 1110 of 1981 (suit for specific performance of contract) instituted Title Suit No. 137 of 1997 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Additional Court, Dhaka. The said Title Suit No. 137 of 1997 was dismissed. On appeal however, in Title Appeal No. 274 of 1998 the learned District Judge Dhaka set aside the judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 137 of 1997 and decreed the suit declaring that the ex parte decree passed in Title Suit No. 1110 of 1981 is illegal, void and not binding upon the Government and the deed bearing No. 18678 dated 20-11-1983 given in Execution Case No. 61 of 1983 is a nullity. It has been further stated that the petitioner filed Title Suit No. 444 of 1984 before the First Court of learned Assistant Judge, Dhaka for declaration that the petitioner is the owner of the property in question and that the same is not Abandoned Property and for recovery of khas possession but the said suit was dismissed on 4-8-1987 by order No. 48. The said order No. 48 and another order No. 47 dated 4-8-1987 were challenged in Civil Revision No. 672 of 1993 before the High Court Division but the Rule was discharged by the judgment and order dated 6-3-2006. It has been further stated that the suit property was under the control and management of the Government as an Abandoned Property since 1972 and that the averments made in the Writ petition are false and fabricated and there is no reason to interfere with the judgment of the First Court of Settlement.

7. In Writ Petition No. 3128 of 1997 it has been stated that the property being No. 16/4, Block- B, Babar Road, Mohammadpur, Dhaka belonged to one Keramat Miah who entered into an agreement on 5-3-1978 for sale of the same to the petitioner but subsequently, he did not execute and register the sale deed and, as such, petitioner was constrained to file Title Suit No. 1108 of 1981 in the Second Court of Subordinate Judge Dhaka for specific performance of contract. The said suit was ultimately decreed ex parte on 8-11-1983 and the sale deed was executed and registered through Court on 25-11-1983 and thereafter the petitioner allegedly got possession of the said house through Court on 12-1-1984. It has been further stated that the Government excluded the said property from the Ka list of Abandoned Buildings and intimated the same to the petitioner vide Memo No. Section 9/1-73/83/1157 dated 28-12-1983 (Annexure-A). It has been further stated that the Government who was one of the defendants of the said suit for specific performance of contract subsequently filed Miscellaneous Case No. 52 of 1985 under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the ex parte decree and thereafter though the matter went to the court of the learned District Judge, Dhaka and thereafter to the High Court Division and subsequently, even to the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, the said ex parte decree was not set aside. In the meantime, the house was included in the Ka list of the Abandoned Buildings and published in the official Gazette on 23-9-1986 and, as such, the petitioner was constrained to file Case No. 765 of 1990 in the First Court of Settlement under section 7 (1) of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 for exclusion of the house from the said list. The Government contested the case in the First Court of Settlement alleging, inter alia, that Keramat Mia was a refugee and the said house was leased out to him for his rehabilitation and that he had left this country during the war of liberation and after the war of liberation one Yousuf Mia was found in possession of the said property and he was given lease of the same with effect from 27-2-1972 and thereafter, the property was also leased out to different persons from time to time.

8. The First Court of Settlement by its judgment and order dated 12-11-1995 dismissed the petitioner's case and refused to exclude the property from the Ka list of Abandoned Buildings and being aggrieved, the petitioner has come to this Court and obtained the present Rule.

9. The respondent No.2, the Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Housing and Public Works, is contesting this Rule by filing Affidavit-in-Opposition denying all the material allegations made in the Writ petition. It was been stated, inter alia, that the property No. 16/4, Block-B, Babar Road, Mohammadpur, Dhaka was leased out by the Government of the then East Pakistan to one Keramat Mia, a refugee, by a registered lease deed dated 22-4-1963 for his rehabilitation. After the war of liberation, the whereabouts of said Keramat Mia was not known and he ceased to occupy the said property and the Government took over control, management and supervision of the property under President's Order 16 of 1972 and allotted the same to one Yousuf Mia by issuing DN on 27-2-1972. Yousuf Mia paid rent to the Government regularly till he left the house in 1975 after which one A Motaleb was given allotment of the same on 13-9-1977. On his transfer to another place, one Habibur Rahman, another Government servant, was given allotment of the said property. Finally, on 24-12-1981, one Mrs Sufia Sultana, an SI of police, was given allotment of the property and she has been paying rent for the same and residing there till date. It has been further stated that the petitioner has created some false documents in respect of the case property and obtained ex parte decree from the court for specific performance of contract. It has been further stated that the original lessee Keramat Mia never entered into any agreement with the petitioner for the alleged transfer of the house and that said Keramat Mia was not present in Bangladesh after Liberation and that he did not receive any consideration money for the case property and, as such, it has been stated that the First Court of Settlement rightly arrived at its decision by dismissing the petitioner's case which calls for no interference by this Court.

10. Mr Fariduddin Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that the owners of the aforesaid two properties entered into two agreements for their sale to the petitioner and thereafter, since the owners did not execute and register the sale deeds, he was constrained to file suits for specific performance of contract in the Court. The Court thereafter passed ex parte decrees and executed sale deeds in his favour and subsequently also delivered possession of the said properties to him. In the said circumstances the First Court of Settlement acted illegally in declaring the aforesaid properties as Abandoned Properties and not excluding it from the Ka list of the abandoned properties. The learned Advocate further submits that the Government issued letters (Annexures-A) to the Writ petitions) clearly stating that the said properties have been excluded from the list of the Abandoned Properties by the Government and, in view of the said memo, the concerned properties ought to be excluded from the list of the Abandoned Properties. The learned Advocate further submits that the Government order dated 28-12-1983 (Annexures-A) releasing the properties in question from the Ka list of the Abandoned Buildings and subsequently, inclusion of the same in the said list on 23-9-1986 is illegal and without jurisdiction.

11. As against this, Mr Adilur Rahman Khan, Deputy Assistant-General, submits that the concerned properties were taken over by the Government as Abandoned Properties just after the war of liberation in 1972 and thereafter, they have been in possession of the Government through different allotees as DN holders. As per provisions of Articles 6 and 14 of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972 (PO 16 of 1972) no transfer of any Abandoned Property can be effected in any manner without getting it released from the list of Abandoned Property and, as such, the petitioner's claim of ownership on the basis of agreements for sale and subsequent ex parte decrees of the Civil Court is misconceived. It has been further submit- ted by the learned Deputy Attorney-General that once the Government shows that any Abandoned Property is in possession of the Government then the onus is upon the claimant to prove that the same is not an Abandoned Property and, in this case, the petitioner has been unable to discharge that burden. The learned Deputy Attorney-General further submits that the Annexure-A to the Writ Petitions are forged documents and that the said papers were never issued by the Ministry of Housing and Public Works and the question of the properties being excluded from the Ka list of Abandoned Properties as alleged does not arise. He further points out that the properties mentioned in the said Annexures are located at Tajmahal Road, Mohammadpur but the properties mentioned in the impugned judgment are located at Babar Road, Mohammadpur and, as such, in any view of the matter Annexure-A in both the Writ petitions have no relevance. He therefore, submits that the judgments passed by the First Court of Settlement calls for no interference by this Court.

12. Mr AY Masihuzzaman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent No.3 in Writ Petition No. 3127 of 1997, submits that the petitioner's claim in the case property in Case No. 20 of 1990 is, inter alia, based upon the ex parte decree obtained in Title Suit No. 1110 of 1981 (the suit for specific performance of contract) but the said decree was set aside in Title Appeal No. 274 of 1998 by the learned District Judge, Dhaka by declaring the same illegal, void and not binding upon the Government, and also holding that deed No. 18675 dated 20-11-1993 given in Title Execution Case No. 61 of 1933 arising out of Title Suit No. 1110 of 1981 was a nullity and therefore, the learned Advocate submits that the petitioner's claim to the property has no leg to stand, He further submits that his client, respondent No. 3, has been possessing the suit property through allotment by the Government and the claim of the petitioner's getting possession of the same through the Court is totally false. He therefore, submits that the instant Rule is liable to be discharged.

13. The petitioner's claims to the concerned properties appear to be primarily based upon two agreements for sale allegedly executed by the owners of the properties and two consequential ex parte decrees by the Civil Court conferring titles in his favour and secondly, two letters (Annexure-A to the Writ petitions), allegedly issued by the Government informing the petitioner that the said properties have been excluded from the Ka list of the Abandoned Buildings.

14. The said properties appear to have been under the control, management and supervision of the Government since 1972 as Abandoned Properties under the provisions of President's Orderl6 of 1972. The petitioner was not able to satisfy the Court of Settlement, that the original allottees were residing in the suit property after 1972 or at the time of executing the Bainapatra with the petitioner. The Court therefore, came to the finding that the aforesaid properties were Abandoned Properties within the meaning of President's Order 16 of 1972 and was in the possession of the Government. The properties being Abandoned Properties as per Article 4 of President's Order 16 of 1972 were not transferable without getting them released from the list of Abandoned Buildings and, as such, found by the Court of Settlement no application was ever filed to have them released from the said list. The petitioner therefore cannot be said to have obtained any interest in the said properties through the alleged decree in the Civil Court on the basis of the alleged agreements for sale.

15. In Writ Petition No. 3128 of 1997 Mr AY Masihuzzaman, the learned Advocate for the respondent No.3, has pointed out that the decree obtained in Title Suit No. 1110 of 1981 pursuant to which the petitioner allegedly obtained title and thereafter Deed No. 18676 dated 20-11-1983 was executed pursuant to Execution Case No. 61 of 1983 was set aside in the Appeal No. 274 of 1998 by the judgment and decree passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka and, in such a situation, the aforesaid Deed No. 18676 dated 20-11-1983 executed pursuant to Execution Case No. 61 of 1983 became a nullity.

16. Furthermore, the petitioner in Writ Petition No. 3128 of 1997 seems to have filed Title Suit No. 444 of 1984 for declaration of title and recovery of khas possession. This indicates that the petitioner was never in possession of the said property. Since the said Title Suit was dismissed it further indicates that the petitioner's claim of being in possession of the property is out and out false.

<u>17. Section 5(2) of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 provides that the lists published under sub-section (1) of section 5 shall be conclusive evidence of the fact that the buildings included therein are abandoned property and have vested in the Government as such. The High Court Division and the Appellant Division upon considering section 5(2) of the aforesaid Ordinance have held in several cases that once a property is listed as an abandoned property the onus lies upon the claimant of the property to prove that it is not an Abandoned Property. Thus, in the instant case, the onus was with the petitioner to prove that on 28th February, 1972 when President's Order 16 of 1972 came into operation and thereafter at the time of the execution of the Bainapatra the original lessees Fouzdar Miah and Keramat Mia were in possession of their respective properties. In the case of the Government of Bangladesh vs law and others reported in 48 DLR (AD) 10 it has been held that the onus is on the claimant of the building to prove that the building is not an Abandoned Property. The Government has no obligation either to deny the facts alleged by the claimant or to disclose the basis of treating the property as Abandoned Property merely because the same is disputed by the claimant. The minimum requirement to satisfy section 5 of the aforesaid Ordinance is, that the Government must show that at some point of time the property in dispute had been taken over as an Abandoned Property by the Government. In both the instant cases, the Court of Settlement found that the Government took over the suit properties as Abandoned Properties and leased them to different persons by issuing DN and the petitioner has failed to discharge the onus cast upon him to disprove the same.</u>

18. As per Annexure-A it is clearly apparent that the properties stated therein are located at Tajmahal Road and not Babar Road. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has tried to explain that due to typing errors Tajmahal Road has been mentioned instead of Babar Road and that it ought to be construed as Babar Road. We find this submission totally unacceptable for being misconceived. It is not for this court to construe a fact when it does not appear on the record. The petitioner could take appropriate steps at the concerned office from where the said memo was issued and get it corrected if there was any typing error. Even during the hearing of these Rules he was given opportunity for at least two weeks to get the same corrected but he failed to do so and we cannot accept that it was a mere typing error. The learned Deputy Attorney-General has stated that the said Annexure-A in both the Writ petitions are forged documents and there is no record of the same having been issued by the concerned Department of the Government. We are constrained to hold that Annexure-A in each of the Writ petitions have got no value and cannot confer any right upon the petitioner.

19. In view of the above, the decrees of the Civil Court against the Government in respect of the abandoned properties have got no binding effect. The judgments and decrees passed by the First Court of Settlement in Case No. 20 of 1990 (Ka 44- Block-B, Babar Road, Dhaka) and Case No. 65 of 1990 (Ka 45 Block B Mohammadpur Dhaka) do not call for any interference by this Court.

20. Accordingly, both the aforesaid Rules are discharged.

There will be no order as to costs.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the defendant-respondent-opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 11-6-2000 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Second Court, Rajbari, in Title Appeal No. 20 of 1996 affirming the judgment and decree dated 30-1-96 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Goalundo, Rajbari, in Title Suit No. 29 of 1994 should not be set aside.

2. The brief fact of the case is, that the plaintiff-appellant-petitioner instituted a suit being Title Suit No. 29 of 1994 in the Court of the Assistant Judge, Goalundo, Rajbari for declaration of title stating, inter alia, that the suit hind measuring, 18 decimal of land originally belonged, to Manu Mallick who mortgaged the said land along with other lands to Rajbari Bank Limited and the Bank purchased the said land through Execution Case No. 731 of 1934 by obtaining a sale certificate from the Court. Thereafter, on 15-1-1944 the plaintiff and his brother Hashmat Ali purchased the above mentioned land by a registered deed and on the same date the plaintiff and his brother sold out the said land to one Mozaharuddin by way of registered kabala deed. Thereafter, the plaintiff got .25 acres of land in Plot No. 940 and 18 decimal of land in Plot No. 922 by a registered pitta dated 29-1-1944 from the said Mozaharuddin and a kabuliat also executed and registered by the plaintiff in favour of Mozaharuddin for the above mentioned total 43 decimal of land on the same date and the reference regarding the said patta was recited in the kabuliat. Thereafter, Mozaharuddin sold out 12 decimal of land from CS Plot No. 912 by executing a registered sale deed dated 30-8-61 where the facts related to the Kabuli at executed by the plaintiff had also been mentioned or narrated. The suit land i.e. 18 acres of land in plot No. 922, is cartilage of the house of the plaintiff and the house was built on the Plot No. 914. The said land is ingress and egress of the plaintiff's house. The plaintiff garages his cattle in the suit land recently, on 15-4-89 corresponding to 2nd Baishakh, 1396 BS the defendant No. 1 through her husband started claiming the suit land baselessly and then plaintiff came to know about the A and RS khatian prepared wrongly in the name of the defendant. The defendant No. 1 has/had no right, title and possession in the suit land in spite of she claimed title in the suit land which constrained the plaintiff to institute the present suit.

3. That the defendant No. 1 respondent-opposite party No. 1 entered appearance and contested the suit by filing written statements denying all the material allegations made in the plaint contending, inter alia that the father of the defendant, No. 1 Abdul Ali Khalifa got the said land by way of pattan from Rajbari Bank Limited and RS Khatian No. 331 was prepared in the name of Abdul Ali Khalifa and he had been paying rent to the said bank for the land on the basis of owner and tenant of the relationship. Thereafter, the suit land was developed under the Government and during SA operation SA record was prepared accordingly, in the name of Abdul Ali Khalifa and he had been possessing the land by cultivating paddy and by cutting the same just before making over the possession of the suit land to defendant No. 1 by executing a registered deed dated 23-6-69. The defendant No.1 used the timber standing on the suit land and her maternal grandmother used to reside there. Presently, the brother of defendant No.1 Enayet Molla looks after the suit land as defendant No. 1 who is residing in Dhaka with her husband. There is no right, title and interest of the plaintiff in the suit land and the records of the suit land has correctly been prepared in the name of the defendant. The defendant No. 1 permitted the plaintiff to use the suit land as pathway to reach the road of Municipal Corporation. The suit has falsely been filed by the plaintiff which is liable to be dismissed with costs.

4. The suit was heard by the learned Assistant Judge, Goalundo, Rajbari and on the basis of the evidence, both oral and documentary, and on the basis of rent receipt and other connected papers, after concluding the trial the learned Assistant Judge, Goalundo, Rajbari was pleased to dismiss the suit by his judgment and decree dated 30-1-96 holding, inter alia, that the suit is not maintainable in its present form; the suit is barred by limitation and defect of parties and RS and SA khatian have correctly been prepared in the name of late Abdul Ali Khalifa having found him in possession of the suit land and that the plaintiff has no right, title and interest in the suit land and also plaintiff has got no exclusive possession in the suit land.

5. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Goal undo, Rajbari the plaintiff preferred an appeal being Title Appeal No. 20 of 1996 in the Court of learned District Judge, which on transfer, was heard by the learned Subordinate Judge, Rajbari who was pleased to dismiss the said appeal by his judgment and decree dated 11-6-2000 and 18-6-2000 respectively holding, inter alia, that it can safely be said that the SA. record was rightly prepared in the name of Abdul Ali Khalifa within the knowledge of the plaintiff and the finding of the trial Court was right and justified as such, he affirmed the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court.

6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Rajbari in Title Appeal No. 20 of 1996, he plaintiff-appellant-petitioner preferred the instant revisional application before the High Court Division and obtained the present Rule.

7. The learned Counsel Mr Syed Mokaddas Ali appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-appellant-petitioner filed a supplementary affidavit adding some new additional grounds to be treated as part of revisional application and submits that the Courts below failed to appreciate the evidence on record and the judgment of both lower appellate Court as well as the trial Court appears to be manifestly perverse affecting the merit of the case resulting failure of justice which is liable to be interfered by this Court. The learned Counsel further submits that the Courts below committed an error in law as well as on facts in deciding the title and possession of the suit land. The learned Courts below without considering the certified copy of the sale deed dated 15-1-1944 executed and registered by Rajbari Bank Limited in favour of the plaintiff which was exhibited as Exhibit 3. Thereafter the certified copy of the registered patta dated 29-1-1944 given by Mozaharuddin in favour of plaintiff Md Shafiuddin which was exhibited as Exhibit 3(A) and the certified copy of the registered kabuliat dated 29-1-1944 given by plaintiff Md Shafiuddin in favour of Mozaharuddin which was exhibited as Exhibit 3(b) and the certified copy of the sale deed dated 15-1-1944 given by plaintiff and another in favour of Mozaharuddin which was exhibited as Exhibit 3(C) the certified copy of the registered sale deed dated 31-8-1961 given by Mozaharuddin in favour of Md Hanifuddin which was exhibited as Exhibit 3(d) were proved by calling the original volumes from the office of the Faridpur District Registrar through PW 5 Abul Hashem Khan and such registered deeds and documents were genuinely executed and hence the tenancy right of the suit land passed to the plaintiff- petitioner. Next he submits that the defendant No. 1 admitted in paragraph No. 13 of the written statements that the CS recorded tenant Manu Mallick was the original owner of the suit land who mortgaged the said land along with other lands to Rajbari Bank Limited and subsequently bank purchased the same through Execution Case No. 731 of 1934 and obtained a sale certificate from the Court. On the other hand the defendant No. 1 claimed the suit land through settlement by the said Rajbari Bank Limited, but neither in the written statement nor in the deposition of DW 1 or any witnesses mentioned any date of such settlement and the defendant could not produce any scrap of paper with regard to the settlement of the suit land on the basis of which the defendant claimed the suit property. The defendant only submits that original deed of pat tan was burned during the liberation war but the defendant could not produce the certified copy or any papers showing that he took paltan from Rajbari Bank Limited. Next the learned Counsel submits that plaintiff examined as many as 5(five) witnesses in this case and defendant also examined 5 witnesses in this case to prove their respective cases but the plaintiff examined the natural, probable and independent witnesses who were neighbours and who categorically stated and corroborated the evidence of PW 1. The PW 4 Md Maznu Miah who is a neighbor of both plaintiff and defendant categorically stated in his evidence that the suit land had been possessed by the plaintiff by grazing his cattle and children of the plaintiff used to play in the suit land, plaintiff also used the suit land as pathway to the access of his house. In cross-examination by the defendant could not shake any of the witnesses and the plaintiff successfully proved the possession of the suit land by adducing evidence. On the other hand, all the five witnesses examined by the defendant are relations. DW 1 Enayet Molla, the full brother of the defendant was examined on behalf of defendant No.1 Most Basera Khatun who in his cross-examination admitted that he could not say when and how and on what date the patta was taken from Rajbari Bank by Abdul Ali Khalifa though he stated that Abdul Ali Khalifa subsequently executed the kabala deed on 23-6-1969 which was exhibited by him as Exhibite-5. Yead Ali and Asfakuddin were examined as DW 2 and DW 3 who were also relations of the defendant. One Abdul Kader, the attesting witness of the deed was examined as DW 4 who stated in his cross-examination that Most Basera Khatun purchased the suit land from her father by a consideration money of Taka 100. He also, admitted that when Basera Khatun purchased the suit land from her father by Taka 100 at that time she was unmarried then where from she got the money. Moniruzzaman was examined as DW 5 who stated in his examination-in-chief that he saw the defendant Abdul Ali Khalifa to possess the suit land but in cross-examination he admitted that Abdul Ali Khalifa died long before i.e. in the year 1975. The learned Counsel for the petitioner further submits that the Courts below did not at all assess the evidence on record properly with regard to the possession of the suit land and came to a wrong and erroneous finding that the defendant was in possession of the suit land but, as a matter of fact, the trial Court as well as the lower appellate Court bank upon the RS and SA khatian and came to the conclusion that if the defendant was not in possession of the suit land the record of SA and RS khatian would not be prepared in the name of the defendant. He further submits that the defendant in collusion with the settlement employee and Tahshilder managed to prepare the khatian in the name of the defendant but the defendant was not in actual possession of the suit land. The lower appellate Court and the trial Court without applying their judicial mind and without proper assessment of the evidence on record and by ignoring the certified copies of series of documents of 1944 showing the title and possession of the plaintiff most illegally dismissed the suit of the plaintiff which is liable to be interfered by this Court. The learned Counsel finally submits that since the original documents were lost during the liberation war the plaintiff submitted the certified copies of all the documents and to prove the genuineness called for the original volume from office of the Faridpur District Registrar through PW 5 Abul Hashem Khan. On the other hand, the defendant could not produce any scrap of paper in support of their claim over the suit land with regard to pattan.

<u>9. The Courts below utterly failed to appreciate the evidence both oral and documentary and by misreading and non-consideration of the evidence came to a wrong finding which is liable to be set aside. In support of his contention the learned Counsel referred the case of Sufia Khatun vs Amin Hossain Mondal and others reported in 10 BLC (AD) 41 wherein it has been held that.</u>

<u>"The law is now settled as to the extent of jurisdiction of the High Court Division under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure to interfere with the judgment of the Court of fact i.e. courts below. The High Court Division in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction is competent to interfere with the judgment of court below only when there is misreading and non-construction of evidence or there is misconstruction of document but when there is no misreading or no consideration of the evidence or when there is no misconstruction of document the High Court Division is not competent to interfere with the judgment of the court below. In the instant case the Courts of fact i.e. the appellate Court and the trial Court, on detailed discussion and consideration of the evidence arrived at the findings that the plaintiff No. 1 has right, title, and possession in the land in suit and the defendants case of taking settlement has not been proved and the dakhilas filed by the defendants in support of the case of taking settlement of the land in suit were not proved by competent, independent and disinterested witnesses. The finding of the High Court Division as regard the possession of the land in suit is not legally well founded".</u>

<u>10. Next he cited another decision in the case of Habibullah (Md) vs Sher Ali Khan and others reported in 57 DLR (AD) 55 it is held that "The High Court Division while exercising its revisional jurisdiction is competent to reverse the judgment of the courts below when the same has been made either upon misreading or non-consideration of the material evidence causing failure of justice". The learned, Counsel referred another decision in the case of Moslem Kha vs Alep Kha and others reported in 10 BLC 708 wherein it is stated that "In a suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession, the trial Court mainly considered the deposition of the DWs ignoring the deposition of the PWs and material documentary evidence which was affirmed by the appellate Court but the High Court Division considered the deposition of the PWs and found that the petitioner had been possessing the suit land since 1966 and accordingly, the suit was decreed setting aside the judgments and decrees of the Courts below". The learned Counsel finally submits that the lower appellate Court and the trial Court committed error in law as well as on facts which arc manifestly perverse, there is serious misreading and non-consideration of material evidence affecting the merit of the case as such, the judgments and decrees passed by the lower appellate Court as well as by the trial Court call for interference by this Court.</u>

<u>11. On the other hand, the learned Counsel Mr Probir Neegi, appearing on behalf of the defendant-respondent-opposite party submits that the concurrent finding of facts cannot be disturbed unless it is manifestly perverse. The trial Court as well as the lower appellate Court is absolutely justified in dismissing the suit of the plaintiff because the plaintiff miserably failed to prove his possession over the suit land and, as such, the Courts below found that the suit is not maintainable and the suit is barred by limitation and it is hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The Courts below rightly found that the plaintiff was not in possession of the suit land and in a suit for declaration the plaintiff cannot .seek any relief as such, the plaintiff ought to have filed a title suit with a prayer for recovery of khas possession. The learned Counsel further submits that the SA and RS Khatian was prepared long before but the plain- tiff did not take any steps for correction of the record if at all it would be wrongly prepared as such the suit of the plaintiff is barred by limitation. The learned Courts below rightly found that the suit was barred by limitation. The defendant examined as many as 5 (five) witnesses in this case to prove the right, title and possession of the suit land and all the DWs proved the case of the defendant with regard to the possession of the suit land. The learned Connsel next submits that both the Courts below concurrently found that the plaintiff Md Shafiuddin Ahmed and his brother Hashmat Ali purchased the suit land along with other land from Rajbari Bank on 15-1-1944 by way of registered deed and on the same day they sold the said property to one Mozaharuddin by a registered deed. Thereafter Mozaharuddin gave patta to the plaintiff by a registered deed dated 29-1-1944 and plaintiff also gave a registered kabuliat to Mozaharuddin on 29-1-1944. The learned Counsel submits that it appears to be an unusual transaction which creates a doubt and suspicion with regard to the genuineness of the document and for this reason the lower appellate Court as well as the trial Court disbelieved the documents. The finding of the Courts below are absolutely right and justified and it should not be disturbed in revision under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In support of his contention the learned Counsel cited the case of Hazari Bala Sana and another vs Niron alias Niranjan Mondal and others reported in 1997 BLD (AD) 295 wherein it has been held that "It is a settled principle that the finding of facts, whether concurrent or not, arrived at by the Power appellate Court, which is the final Court of fact, is binding on the High Court Division, as a revisional to out except in certain well defined exceptional circumstances, such as non-consideration or misreading of the material evidence affecting the merit of the case. Finally, the learned Counsel submits that if the plaintiff would be in possession of the suit land certainly the RS and SA Khatian would be prepared in the name of the plaintiff and; as such, both the Courts below rightly observed that the plaintiff miserably failed to prove his right; title and possession over the suit land. Therefore the judgment passed by the Courts below do not call for any interference by this Court.</u>

12. On a meticulous examination of the judgment of lower appellate Court as well as the, trial Court and evidence on record and also the exhibits it transpires that both the Courts below erred in law as, well as on facts. Both the Courts below gave much emphasis on a very immaterial point i.e. the plaintiff along with his brother purchased the suit land from Rajbari Bank and on the same day they sold out the land to one Mozaharuddin which appeared, to them very, much unusual as such, the Courts below disbelieved all the documents of the plaintiffs. This observation made by the Courts below are not whole good because there is no legal bar to purchase a property from somebody and again to sell the property to anybody. It may so happen that due to exigency of circumstances the plaintiff may purchase and again sell the property to, somebody, The finding of the Courts below in respect of possession is not at all correct because plaintiff has examined 5 witnesses in this case who were neighbours and natural, independent and probable witnesses of the case and not at all interested witnesses who categorically proved the possession of the suit land by the plaintiff. Particularly the PW 4 who is a close neighbor of both plaintiff and defendant stated in his deposition that the plaintiff has been possessing the suit land since long by grazing cattle and his children used to play in the suit land and the plaintiff used the suit land as pathway to enter into his house. On the other hand, defendant also examined 5 witnesses who are all related to defendant and highly interested except DW 4 Abdul Kader who stated in his deposition that he was an attesting witness of the kabala deed when the suit land was purchased by Basera Khatun from her father at a consideration of Taka 100. But in cross-examination Abdul Kader admitted that when defendant purchased the suit land at that time she was unmarried and wherefrom she got the money to purchase the suit land she could not explain and, as a matter of fact, no consideration money was transited; The defendants claimed that they got the property from Rajbari Bank as pattan but not a single scrap of papers was produced by the DWs that the suit land was given as pattan by the Rajbari Bank in the name of Abdul Ali Khalifa. The defendant produces only SA and RS khatians showing their possession in the suit land. In this connection I rely on the case of Md Yasin and others vs Kamini Kumar Shome being dead his heirs namely Prothad Shome and others reported in 2 BCR 217 passed by a Division Bench wherein it was held that-

"If need not be said again that mere payment of rent to the Government on the strength of unfounded entry in the record of right will not create a valid tenancy in favour of the defendants and extinguish title if any of the plaintiff No.1".

<u>13. The Courts below failed to apply their judicial mind to assess the evidence both oral and documentary on record properly as such came to a wrong finding and dismissed the suit of the plaintiff. Both the Courts below by misreading and non-consideration of the material evidence both oral and documentary affecting the merit of the case with regard to title and possession of the plaintiff and failed to come to a correct finding of the case which is liable to be interfered by this Court. The plaintiff in proving his title produced the certified copy of the title deed and called the volume from the District Registrar Office to prove the genuineness of the documents since the original document was lost during the liberation war. 'The plaintiff also proved his title and possession over the suit and by adducing evidence of disinterested and independent witnesses who could not be shaken in cross examination by the defendant as such the judgment' and decree passed by the Courts below is called for interference by this Court. In this connection I like to rely on the case of Habibullah (Md) vs Sher Ali Khan and others reported in 57 DLR (AD) 55 wherein it has been held that "The High Court Division while exercising its revisional jurisdiction is competent to reverse the judgment of the Courts below when the same has been made either upon misreading or non-consideration of the material evidence causing failure of justice. Another decision can also be cited in this connection in the case of Hussain Ahmed Chowdhury alias Ahmed Hossain Chowdhury and others vs Md Nurul Amin and others reported in 47 DLR (AD) 162 wherein it is stated that</u>

<u>"If there is misreading of evidence and non-consideration of some material evidence then it was incumbent on the revisional Court to consider the same and to arrive at a proper finding on the material evidence on record and to finally dispose of the case"</u>

14. It will not be out of place to cite another decision with regard to Registration Act, Section 60 of the Registration Act and sections 65(c), 68, 78 and 79 of the Evidence Act, in the case of Aboni Mohan Saha vs Assistant Custodian, Vested Property, Chandpur reported in 39 DLR (AD) 223 wherein it is held that the proof of certified copies and presumption as to genuineness of the same when a certified copy of the document is produced some sanctity of law is attested by the Evidence Act "Section 78 read with section 79 of the Evidence Act provides for the proof of' the certified copies and the presumption as to the genuineness of such certified copies. The plaintiff has given explanation that the original was burnt.

Section 65(c) provides for secondary evidence "When the original has been destroyed or lost, or when the party offering evidence of its contents cannot, for any other reason not arising from his own default or neglect, produce it in reasonable time." It is further provided in cases of (a), (c) and (d) that secondary evidence of the contents of the document is admissible when the certified copy was produced by the plaintiff of registered deed of gift.

The certified, copy could not be brushed aside in the way it has been done by the courts below. It is unfortunate that even the courts did not notice section 68 of the Evidence Act which provides as to the mode of proof of the execution of document required by law to be attested and the law is that it shall not be used as evidence until one attesting witness has been called for the purpose of proving execution if there be an attesting witness alive and capable of giving evidence and adds an exception by way of proviso:

"provided that it shall not be necessary to call an attesting witness if proof of the execution of any document, not being a will, which has been registered in accordance' with the provisions of the Indian Registration Act, 1908, unless its execution by the person by whom it purports to have been, executed is specifically denied."

Section 59, Evidence Act

Reliance on oral evidence of the interested witnesses in utter disregard of the principles of Law of Evidence deprecated:

Reliance of oral evidence of the interested witnesses in utter disregard of the principles propounded by the law of Evidence tantamount to open a door for extraneous considerations thereby jeopardising judicial thinking and its process. There is always the danger in a case like the, present that conjecture or suspicion may take the place of legal proof.

15. In view of the discussion made above and the facts and circumstances of the case and also the legal position, the plaintiff is entitled to obtain a decree in his favour. I find that the lower appellate Court is absolutely wrong in dismissing the Title Appeal No. 20 of 1996 arising out of the judgment and decree dated 30-1-1996 and also the judgment and decree passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Goalundo, Rajbari, in Title Suit No. 29 of 1994. The judgment and decree dated 11-6-2000 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 2nd Court, Rajbari, in Title Appeal No. 20 of 1996 affirming the judgment and decree Gated 30-1-96 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Goalundo, Rajbari, in Title Suit No. 29 of 1994 is hereby set aside.

16. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to the costs. The judgment and decree of both the Courts below are set aside and accordingly, the suit is decreed in favour of the plaintiff.

Lower Courts records be sent down at once with a copy of judgment.

End.

Vs.
