full_judgment:
Siddiqur Rahman Miah J: This revisional application along with Civil Rule No. 928(R) of 2005 and Civil Rule No. 17(R) of 2006 are taken together for disposal.

2. This revisional application under section 115 (1) of the Code of Civil Procedure at the instance of the defendant-respondent is directed against the judgment and decree dated 31-3-2004 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Chandpur in Title Appeal No. 41 of 2000 allowing the appeal by reversing the judgment and decree dated 2-3-2000 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Chandpur in Title Suit No. 36 of 1994 dismissed the suit.

3. The opposite party No.1, Gazi Golam Mahammad, as plaintiff filed Title Suit No: 36 of 1994 in the court of Subordinate Judge, Chandpur for declaration of title in the suit land.

4. The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that the suit land appertaining to an area of 0.05 acres in plot No. 931 under CS khatian No. 242 corresponding to SA Khatian No. 229 and 0.06 acres in both former and present plot No. 931/969 of mouza Dasadi under both District and police station Chandpur has been owning and possessing by Durga Kumar Chakraborty and others from their predecessor namely, Shamkanti Das alias Shamcharan Chakraborty that the plaintiff, namely Gazi Nur Mohammad (now dead) brought Title Suit No. 324 of 1958 in the court of Munsif, first court at Chandqur ( relating to non, suit land) for specific performance of contract, whereupon the decree was passed on 4-4-1961 in favour of the plaintiff with Taka 417.50 as cost; that thereafter said Nur Mohammad obtained registered deed on 11-5-1963 through court: that Nur Mohammad, then filed an execution Case bearing No. 72 of 1963 for realisation of the alleged cost money; that the plaintiff also purchased the land in suit along with other land in auction as highest bidder and also took Bainama on 26-1-1992; that 931 Khatian was mentioned wrongly in that execution case in place of correct CS khatian No. 242 or SA khatian No. 229 and plot No.931-931/969 but the boundary mentioned in auction was intact and that the possession of the land was handed over to plaintiff on 30-4-1992 with performing all formalities of auction sale and thus the case for execution of decree bearing No. 72 of 1963 was disposed of on 31-5-1992 with full satisfaction and since then the plaintiff has been possessing and enjoying its interest by himself as well as by his tenants. It is further stated that the plaintiff namely, GaziNur Mohammad died during pendency of Execution case No. 72 of 1963 and his heirs namely, Hayet-un-nessa and others were substituted in the case; that the defendant refused and threw challenge over the right and status of the plaintiff on the suit land on 16-9-1994 on the basis of a decree in a title suit bearing No. 468 of 1982 and also threatened to dispossess them and for which the plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 128 of 1994 for permanent injunction; that the suit was filed in wrong forum for which he finally withdrew the same. It is further stated that the Deputy Commissioner and others on behalf of the government of Bangladesh filed another suit being No. 34 of 1992 praying for declaring the alleged auction and the decree in execution case No. 72 of 1963 as illegal, not binding upon and collusive but the suit was ultimately dismissed.

5. The defendant No. 1 namely Abdus Satter Mizi who is present petitioner and on behalf of Government, defendant Nos. 5 and 6 i.e. Deputy Commissioner and Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev) Chandpur respectively contested the suit by filing written statement separately. The case of the defendant No.1, in short, is that the total area of land in khatian No. 242 is 12 decimals containing 5 decimals in plot No. 931 and 7 decimals in plot No.931/969 has been owning and possessing by Shamkanto Das and Nibaran Chandra Das, eight annas each, as Rayeti interest and later on Shamkanto Das sold his portion to one Suresh Chandra Chakraborty and accordingly, SA khatian was published in their names; that the defendant took lease on 2 decimals of land including shops thereon in plot No. 931 and that Suresh Chandra Chakraborty left this country and went to India, as such, this defendant took lease of the property, left by Suresh Chandra Chakraborty from Sub-Divisional Officer, vide VP Case No. 8/82-83 and paying rent thereof from 1373 BS to 1380 BS at the rate of Taka 400 per year and from 1381 BS to 1389 BS at the rate of Taka 800 per year. This defendant also paid UP tax and doing business procuring licence and setting electric meter thereto.

6. It is further stated that the defendant has been threatened by some Nur Islam, Abdul Bepari and Kasim Patari on 30-11-1982 and in order to resist them he filed Title Suit No. 468 of 1982 for permanent injunction and during pendency of that suit; that the defendant was dispossessed from the land as such prayed for mandatory injunction and that the suit was dismissed, on which, an appeal was preferred and the same was allowed and that thereafter the defendant of that suit went to the High Court and filed a Civil Revision which was discharged.

7. It is further stated that the plaintiff did not file any case for execution of decree bearing No. 72 of 1963 and no auction took place and that all are paper transactions; that the plaintiff has no right, title and interest in the suit land and the plaintiff filed the suit falsely which is liable to be dismissed.

8. The defendant Nos. 5 and 6, on behalf of the Government, stated in their written statement that the suit land measuringan area of 0.05 acres in plot No. 931 under SA khatian No. 229 and Mouza 18 Dasadi under police station and District Chandpur and 0.06 acres in plot No. 931/969 is vested property; that 0,02 acres of land of plot No. 931 and 0.03 acres of plot No. 931/969 i.e. in total 0.05 acres of land has been leased out to defendant No: 1 vide LA Case No. 08 of 1982-83; that LA Case No.3 of 1981-83; that 21 of 1982-83 and that since the lease property is under possession and control of government, the case of the plaintiff should be dismissed.

9. The learned trial Court framed the following issues:

1 Whether the suit is maintainable in its present form?

2. Whether the, title of the plaintiff in suit land through auction purchase is to be declared?

3. Whether the judgment and decree in title suit No.486 of 1982 be declared as not binding upon the plaintiff?

4. Whether the suit of the plaintiff is bad by defendant of parties?

5. Whether the suit is barred by law of limitation and

6. Whether the plaintiff is entitled to get decree as prayed for?

10. On examination of record, it transpires that the plaintiff appellant examined as many as 4 witnesses, excluding himself and the contesting defendant No. 1 produced a single witness excluding himself and one Mohamrnadullah Tahshilder, was examined on behalf of the defendant Nos. 5 and 6.

11. The plaintiff filed a certified copy of CS khatian marked Exhibit 1, a copy Of SA khatian marked Exhibit 2, certified copy of judgment of the suit No. 324 of 1958 marked as Exhibit 3, Original registered deed No. 4239 dated 11-5-1963 with respect to title execution case No.7 of 1962 marked as Exhibit 4, Petition for the title execution case No. 72 of 1963 in the Munsif, First Court, Chandpur marked Exhibit-5, Original Boinama as regard auction purchase in said execution case marked Exhibit 6, certified copy of writ of execution marked Exhibit 6(ka), certified copy of the plaint of title suit No. 34 of 1992 marked Exhibit 7(ka), certified copy of the order dated 7-7-1992 of suit marked as Exhibit 7 (kha), information slip as regard title suit No. 468 of 1982 marked Exhibit 8 and certified copy of the judgment of the Additional District Judge in Miscellaneous Appeal No.9 in 1995 marked Exhibit 9 in support of his contention.

12. On the other hand, defendant No. 1 has submitted certified copy of CS khatian No. 242 marked Exhibit-Ka, certified copy of the SA khatian No. 229 marked as Exhibit ka(1), report dated 21-8-1982 by Tahashilder in VP Case marked as Exhibit- Kha, 2 sheets of DCR as regard rent marked Exhibit-GA, One trade licence marked Exhibit-Gha, certified copy of the judgment and decree in title suit No. 71 of 1985 marked as Exhibit-Oma, certified copy of the order of Civil Revision No. 247 of 1886 (Comilla)/8916 of 1991 (Dhaka) dated 27-3-1994 marked Exhibit-Cha and certified copy of the order dated 19-5-1994 in his case marked Exhibit- Cha(1) in support of his contention.

13. The defendant Nos. 5 and 6 filed attested photo copy of the list of rent roll by Abdus Satter Mizi as Exhibit A(a), Order sheet, petition, enquiry report, map of VP case No. 3 of 1981-82, 21, of 1982-83 are marked Exhibit Aa/1 in support of their contention.

14. The learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Chandpur considering the facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record dismissed the suit by, his order dated 2-3-2000.

15. Being aggrieved by the impugned judgment and decree dated 2-3-2000, the plaintiff preferred Title Appeal being No. 41 of 2000 in the court of the learned District Judge, Chandpur and on transfer, the appeal was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, Chandpur who considering the facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record allowed the appeal reversing the judgment and decree dated 2-3-2000.

16. The respondent being aggrieved RY the impugned judgment and decree dated 31-3-2004 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Chandpur in title Appeal No. 41 of 2000 as the petitioner filed this revisional application before this court and obtained the present Rule.

17. The point for determination is, whether the learned Additional District Judge, Chandpur committed any error of law in passing the judgment and decree dated 31-3-2004 and" which caused any failure of justice.

18. Mr Abul Hossain Sarder, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the learned trial Court after considering the facts and material on record having found that the Schedule of the auction purchased land as per boinama as Exhibit 6 dated 26-1-1992 does not tally or is not identical with the suit land as mentioned in the, schedule of the plaint and thus dismissed the suit; that the learned appellate Court without considering the schedule of the boinama held that the suit land is identical with the schedule of the boinama that the trial Court having found that the identity of the suit land having riot been established by local investigation, the suit cannot be decreed and accordingly, dismissed the suit and that, on the other hand, the appellate Court though found that the khatian No. 931 in the boinama was wrong but held that the boundary of the auction purchased land was properly given-in the, boinama overlooking the fact that only the north and south boundary have been mentioned, not all sides have been mentioned in the said boinama and thus the learned appellate Court committed an error in allowing the appeal. He 'further submits that the learned trial Court considering the evidence of PWs and DWs held that the plaintiff failed to prove his possession in the suit land and thus dismissed the suit; that the learned. Appellate Court did not consider properly the evidence of PWS and DWs on record and committed an error of law in allowing the appeal holding that since the plaintiff go possession the suit land before, through court in execution case, there is little scope for ascertaining possession further and that the learned appellate Court committed an error in allowing appeal occasioning failure of justice;

19. Mr TM Shakil Hossain, the, learned Advocate for the opposite parties, submits. that the representative of government, Deputy Commissioner, Chandqur, filed Title Suit No. 34 of 1992 for canceling the auction sale in that suit; that the Government did not deny that the, suit land and plaintiff's auction purchased land are not same; that as such, the petitioner of the Civil Revision who is merely a lessee of government has no right to raise the question that the suit land is not auction purchased land and that the government did not prefer any revision before the High Court against the judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court meaning thereby government has admitted the land in suit as property of opposite party No. 1, as such, the petitioner being a lessee under the government has no interest in the suit land. He further submits that the trial Court though dismissed the suit but after considering the materials on record came to the finding that the defendant No. 1 that is, the present petitioner, has no interest in the land in suit which was affirmed by the learned appellate Court and against that finding, petitioner did not file any cross appeal or objection as such the court in exercising its revisional jurisdiction cannot interfere with the concurrent finding.

20. Mr TM Shakil Hossain, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, cited the decision in the case of Sajiuddin Kazi alias Sajiruddin vs Moslem Ali Howlader and others reported in 12 DLR 266; in the case of Md Alkas Ali and others vs Mansur Ahmed Khan and others reported in 1983 BLD (AD) 126; in the case of Mojizullah Bhuiyan and others vs Sree Narayan Chandra Roy and others reported in 3 MLR (AD) 196; in the case of Moulana Abdul Matin and others vs Shah Alam Bhuiyan and others reported in 41 DLR 243; in the case of Government of Bangladesh vs Paresh Chandra Gharalizi and others reported in 50 DLR (AD) 70; in the case of Abdul Quddus vs Mr Nizamudin Ahmed Advocate and others reported in 4 MLR (AD) 129 = 51 DLR (AD) 103; in the case of Kayomat Ali Sikdar and others vs Jainuddin Talukder reported in 14 DLR 657 and in the case-of Commander (Retd) AA Chowdhury vs AKM Imam Hossain and others reported in 49 DLR 23 in support of his contention.

21. Before coming to the decision in the instant Civil Revision No. 1074 of 2004, we like to dispose of the Civil Rule 17(R) of 2006. This rule relates to an application (cross objection) under section XLI, rule 22 of the Code of Civil Procedure and this rule was tiled out of time by 486 days in which Rule was issued upon the opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the delay of 486 days in filing the Rule should not be condoned. In reply, the opposite party No. 1 filed counter affidavit stating that Md Abdul Mannan Mal, son of Abdul Gafur Mal, the 3rd party petitioner No. 1 on 24-2-2000 deposed in the suit as DW 2, as such, it is crystal clear that 3rd party petitioner had full knowledge about the suit but by suppressing the said facts the petitioner has obtained this Rule being Civil Rule No. 17(R) of 2006 which has no merit.

22. On the other hand, Abdul Mannan Mal stated in this rule application that the delay is unintentional and beyond his control and, as such, he prayed for condonation of delay.

23. Since the petitioner, Abdul Mannan Mal, deposed as DW 2 in original suit, so it is quite clear that he was aware of the matter. As such the delay cannot be condoned and consequently the Rule being No. 17(R) of 2006 is discharged without any order as to cost.

24. Now we come back to our revision in which pertinent question that calls for our determination is, whether the petitioner actually auction purchased the suit land on 22-10-1991 although there was some wrong in plot arid khatian.

25. The plaintiff petitioner claims that the suit No. 324 of 1958 was decreed on 4-4-1961 with cost of Taka 471.50 marked Exhibit-3 and the suit land was auction sold through execution case No. 72 of 1963 for realisation of cost money filed by the plaintiff's father and the suit was attached on 15-11-1963 (Exhibit 3) and the petitioner purchased the same on 22-10-1991 and the sale was confirmed on 20-1-1992 and Boinama was prepared on 26-1-1992 (Exhibit 6). The further case of the plaintiff is that the plaintiff got possession of the land through court noting therewith having the execution case disposed of as satisfactorily. There cord, especially, of Exhibit 5 and 6 seriess prove the submissions as referred by learned Advocate for plaintiff-petitioner.,

26. It is, therefore, clear that the judgment and decree in original title suit No. 324 of 1958 (Exhibit-3) and their effectiveness and validity remain intact and untouched.

27. It is further found that the government represented by Deputy Commissioner, Chandpur filed Title suit No. 34 of 1992 for cancellation of auction sale but the government did not deny that the suit land and the plaintiff auction purchased land is not same, as such, the petitioner of the present revision who is a lessee of the government has no right to raise the question that the suit land is not auction purchased land.

28. It further appears that the government did not prefer any revision before this court against the judgment and decree passed by the learned appellate Court meaning thereby government has admitted the land in suit as property of plaintiff opposite party No.1; as such, the petitioner-has no right in the suit.

29 . There is no denial of the facts that the trial Court though dismissed the suit but on considering the material on record came to the finding that the defendant No. 1 lessee, has no interest in the land it suit which was affirmed by the learned appellate Court and against that finding petitioner did not file any cross appeal or objection, as such, this court in exercising its revisional power cannot interfere with the concurrent finding of both the courts below.

<u>30. The moot point for determination is, whether the plaintiff actually got possession of the suit land through auction purchase is admitted that there were some mistakes both in execution case and boinama. But in the boinama there was mentioning of boundary in two sides. The consistent view of our Apex court is that the case of dispute between the plot and khatian, boundary will prevail. Our Appellate Division in the case of Mofizullah Bhuiyan and others vs Sree Narayan Chandra Roy and others reported in 3 MLR (AD) 196 held that when the plaintiffs succeed in proving their title and possession in the suit, land, they are entitled to get a decree for declaration of his title therein. The suit cannot be dismissed merely on the ground of minor variations in the description of the boundaries of the suit land.</u>

31. In the instant case, though there is some variations in plot and khatian but there is boundary in the boinama which proves that the suit land is identical with the auction purchased land. Moreover, the present petitioner who is a lessee has no legal right raised this point of variation as the government lost in suit No. 34 of 1992 on this point and the government did not appeal to the higher court against the judgment and decree and thus the government or his lessee is debarred from raising this point any more.

32. Moreso, both the courts below upon appreciation of evidence on record came to the finding that the land in suit is not vested property and government did neither file any cross objection nor did prefer any appeal against those judgments as such this revisional court cannot interfere with the said concurrent findings of fact. Moreover, it appears from the evidence on record that the learned appellate Court after elaborate discussion, both oral and documentary evidence, arrived at a correct finding by reversing the finding of the trial Court.

33. The learned Additional District Judge, Chandpur as a final court of facts, on consideration of all material aspects of the case and material evidence on record rightly allowed the appeal reversing the judgment and decree dated 2-3-2000. The learned Additional District Judge was fully justified in allowing the appeal. on assigning cogent and good reason, as such, the impugned judgment and decree do not suffer from any illegality and legal infirmity so as to justify interference by this court exercising revisional power under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

34. In the result the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs and the impugned judgment and decree dated 31-3-2004 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Chandpur in title Appeal No. 41 of 2000 is hereby affirmed.

35. Connected rule being Civil Rule No. 928 (R) of 2005 regarding status quo and Civil Rule No. 17(R) of 2006 are also hereby discharged and vacated.

Send down the LCR at once.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 9th June, 1997 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3179 of 1993).
full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Karim J: Plaintiff has filed this petition for leave to appeal against judgment and order dated 9 June, 1997 of the High Court Division making the Rule absolute in Civil Revision No. 3179 of 1993 setting aside those dated 12-6-93 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge allowing Miscellaneous Judicial Case No. 3 of 1993 reviewing his earlier judgment dated 3-3-1993 in Other Class Appeal No.179 of 1991 under Order 47 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. The suit was for declaration that the plaintiff was illegally and wrongfully dismissed from his service on 27-1-77 and that he was entitled to be reinstated with full arrear dues up-to-date. The short fact stating, inter alia, that the petitioner appointed as a Stenographer was absorbed and promoted to the rank of Branch Manager and on transfer to join his place of transfer allowed 7 day’s time but due to illness of the mother and on reaching home found her condition serious. Petitioner sent application for leave for 4 months with a request to forward the same to the General Manager, Dhaka. But the Regional Manager did not forward the same instead brought charge on 14-6-1976 asking him to file explanation to the Enquiry Officer who as well asked him to appear before him on 9-7-1976. The petitioner appeared and filed explanation denying the allegation of absence without leave and behavior of insubordination and unbecoming manner, disobeying lawful order of superior and exhibiting an irresponsible character. The petitioner was dismissed from service on 26-1-1977 against which an appeal was as well rejected. An application of the petitioner before the Managing Director to reinstate was of no effect whereupon the petitioner sent a notice alleging his wrongful dismissal from service in violation of principle of natural justice. The defendant denied the allegation stating that the reply to the charges were not satisfactory and full opportunity was given and the charges brought against him having been proved beyond reasonable doubt, he was legally dismissed from service from complying with the law and the procedure.

3. The suit was initially decreed and on appeal the same was sent on remand. Thereafter the suit was again decreed ex parte against which defendant preferred an appeal which was allowed on contest restoring the suit to its file and number vacating the ex parte decree. The suit was again decreed against which an appeal was preferred which was allowed on 3-3-1993 dismissing the suit. Against the said decree in appeal the plaintiff- petitioner preferred a review petition being Miscellaneous Judicial Case No. 3 of 1993 which was allowed by judgment and order dated 12-6-1993. The defendant, however, preferred revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure making the Rule absolute setting aside the judgment in review. Against the said judgment and order dated 9-6-1997 the petitioner moved this Court with this petition.

4. Mr Moksudur Rahman, learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner, submitted that the High Court Division erred in law in not holding that whether the error crept through Court's oversight or counsel mistake if it is apparent on the face of the record it could be cured without driving to the appeal and misconception of fact and/or law of the learned Advocate is sufficient reason for review inasmuch as the High Court Division has misconceived the scope and purpose of Order XLVII rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

<u>5. Order XLVII rule 1 of the CPC contemplates a review of a judgment and order on discovery of new and important matter which was not known or could not be produced or on account of mistake or error of the record or any other substantial cause. Review is therefore by no means an appeal in disguise whereby an erroneous decision is reheard or corrected but lies only on patent error. In the instant case the review was sought for on the ground of misapplication of certain decision cited to hold that the suit is not maintainable with principle that the petitioner's service is guided by master servant rule. Omission to place the relevant decision at the hearing of the suit or at the appeal is not mistake or error apparent on the face of the record so as to invoke the provision of Order XLVII rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure having disposed of the suit on merit. There cannot be rehearing or further hearing of the suit which is already concluded by the decision if any that be erroneous to invoke the provision of review unless the mistake or error is apparent on the face of the record. Mere wrong application of law is no ground of review and if it be allowed to do then the scope of appeal would be frustrated. A suit allegedly decreed on the basis of cited decision which even if meanwhile reversed is no ground for review.</u>

6. The High Court Division, in the facts and circumstances of the case, rightly held that "Having regard to the aforesaid decision and in view of the facts and circumstances of the case I find that the learned Additional District Judge, Mr Soumendra acted illegally in sitting over his own judgment by entertaining the Miscellaneous review application to rehear the appeal already concluded by decision even if that be erroneous."

In view of the above, the petition is dismissed.

End.

full_judgment:
Md Joynul Abedin J: This Rule Nisi on an application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned Judgment and order dated 21-9- 2000 passed by the First Court of Settlement, Dhaka in Settlement Case No. 92 of 1998" Ka 280 Block-D, Mohammadpur, Dhaka should not be declared to have been passed without any' lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

2 It is stated in the petitioner that a vacant land comprising 140 square yards situated at Mouza Dakhin Adabar and Barabo, PS Tejgaon now Mohammadpur on which House No. XXV/8; in Block-D of Layout Plan No. 127 1960-61 is standing now was originally allotted to one Md Yasin, son of Noor Ainon on hire-purchase basis vide allotment order No. 2033/CHS dated 22-5- 1961 by the erstwhile Government of East 'Pakistan on certain terms and conditions. Subsequently, a lease deed No. 7768 dated 14-12-61 was executed and registered by the then Government of East Pakistan in favour of Md Yasin and possession thereof was formally handed over to him and Yasin had been continuing in possession since then Thereafter said Md Yasin having observed all formalities transferred the said house property to Shamirn Ahmed and Nasim Ahmed by a registered sale deed No. 7668 dated 7-8-69. While said Shamim Ahmed and Nasim Ahmed were continuing as owner in possession of the said house property with the petitioner. Since said Shamim Ahmed and Nasim Ahmed failed to execute and register necessary sale deed in favour of the First Court of Subordinate Judge for specific performance, of contract. against the said two vendors and the Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works. The said suit was eventually decreed ex parte in favour of the petitioner on 14-4-79 directing the aforesaid vendors, namely Shamim Ahmed and Nasim Ahmed, to execute and register necessary sale deed in favour of the petitioner within 6 (six) days on receipt of the balance consideration money, Since the said vendors failed to execute and register necessary sale deed, necessary sale deed was executed and registered by the executing court in Execution Case No. 23 of 1979 on 9-4-80 being sale deed No. 14770 dated 22-4-80. Thereafter, the executing court also handed over possession of the said property to the petitioner through its Nabi Nazir and process server on 9-11-80, by evicting the representatives of the judgment debtor, Nasiruddin, Profullah Chandra Roy and Wadud.

3. The petitioner thereafter applied to the Deputy Commissioner, Housing and Settlement Department on 14-3-83 for mutation of his name on the records as owner, the Ministry of Works thereafter by a memo dated 12-11-84 asked the petitioner to appear before the DS AP-2, within 7 days with documents and the petitioner thereupon submitted basic documents of title showing his ownership and requested for mutation Of his name, Instead of mutating the names of the petitioner, the government filed Miscellaneous Case No. 31 of 1986 on 23-2-1986 for setting aside the said ex parte decree under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Eventually, the said Miscellaneous Case was also dismissed by the Court on 14-3-1988 for default as the Government did not take any step. In this background of the case, the petitioner has been residing on the said house property since the possession thereof was handed over to him by the court on 9-11-90. But the government thereafter surreptitiously enlisted the said house property of the petitioner in the Ka "list" as abandoned building although the petitioner is in possession of the same. Accordingly, the petitioner filed Settlement case No. 92/88(Ka-Block-D, Mohammadpur) to exclude the said house property from the " Ka" list of abandoned property. The Court of Settlement, subsequently on misconstruction of facts and law in the matter rejected the case of the petitioner refusing to exclude the same from the "Ka" list on the finding that it was an abandoned property by the impugned Judgment and order dated 31-9-2000.

4. The respondent No. 1 contested the Rule by filing the affidavit-in-opposition.

5. We have heard the learned Advocate Mr Abul Kalam Chowdhury for the petitioner and Mr Zaman Akhter Bulbul, the learned Assistant Attorney General for the respondents. We have perused the writ petition as well as the affidavit-in-opposition along with the Annexures thereto.

<u>6. Admittedly, the petitioner obtained decree dated 14-4-79 from the civil Court for specific performance of contract and subsequently obtained a registered sale deed dated 22-4-1980 in respect of the house property in favour of the petitioner through Court. Subsequently, the petitioner also obtained possession of the said house property on 9- 11-1980 through Court. The respondents i.e. the government has not denied this factual position. It is therefore an established position that the government, was not in possession of the said house property directly or constructively through its tenant or allotted since 9-11-1980. In this background of the case, the Court of Settlement has failed to take note of the said legal and factual position that the petitioner had obtained a sale deed in respect of the said house property from a competent Court showing the valid agreement for sale. The government did not take any step to set aside the said decree and recover possession of the house through court. The government did not take  possession of the said house property from the petitioner by evicting him therefrom giving requisite notice in this regard as contemplated under Article 7(2) and (3) of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property Order, 1972 (PO 16 of 1972). The Court of Settlement has also fallen in error in failing to consider the legal position that the government was not competent to take over possession and enlist the said house property in the "Ka'' list under section 5(1) (a) of the Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 without issuing any notice under section 4 of the said Ordinance, 1985 asking the petitioner to surrender possession of the said house. The Court an the Judgment and decree dated 14-4- 1979 passed by the civil Court in the suit for specific performance as would be evident from the following observation and finding of the Settlement Court.</u>

<u>"প্রার্থীর বায়াগন.............. স্বাধীনতা যুদ্ধের সময় হইতে পরবর্তী সময়ে এদেশে ছিলেন বা আছেন ....... প্রমাণ করিতে পারে নাই। নালিশী সম্পত্তিতে দখলের বিষয়ে সমর্থন যোগ্য প্রমাণ করা হয় নাই। .......এবং তদমর্মে উপরোল্লিখিত দেওয়ানী মকদ্দমায় একতরফা ডিক্রি হাসিল করিয়াছেন বলিয়া মনে করি।</u>

The respondents in their affidavit-in-opposition has not stated anything about taking over of possession of the said house property at any time between 28-2-70 and the date of inclusion of the  same in the "ka" list. The petitioner, on the other hand, has asserted that he went into possession of the said house on 9-4-1980. The Government was  therefore under legal obligation to establish that it formed an opinion that the said house was lying vacant and uncared for as its owners were not present in Bangladesh from before 28-2-1972 and it took it over as an abandoned property and subsequently the government being in possession enlisted the said house in the ka list. But the government has failed to do so. Mere statements of the respondents that whereabouts of the original lessee, Md Yasin or his vendors Shamim Ahmedand NasimAhmed were not present in Bangladesh from  28-2-1972 will not absolve the government in law from taking appropriate steps setting aside the said sale deed and taking over the possession of the said house property by issuing requisite notice as contemplated under Article 7(2) and (3) of  President's Order 16 of 1972 and also under sections 4 and 5(1) (a) of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985. The Court of Settlement has wrongly approached these problems as if it was a court for determination of title of the said house property. In this regard, the case reported in 9 MLR 76 may be cited. The impugned judgment and order of the Court of Settlement, in our view, is therefore liable to be declared without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

7. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The impugned Judgment and order dated 21-9-2000 passed by the First Court of Settlement in Case No. 92 of 1988 (Ka 280 Block-D, Mohammadpur, Dhaka) is set aside.

The respondents are directed to exclude the house in question from the "Ka" list of the abandoned buildings within 2 months from the date of receipt of this order.

End.

full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Karim J: This appeal by leave arose out of the judgment and order dated 24th August, 2003 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1476 of 2003 making the Rule absolute-in-part so far as it relates to finding in respect of section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and directing the, Court to dispose of the question of maintainability of the suit before recording of the evidence setting aside the order dated 27-2-2003 passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Savar, Dhaka in title Suit No. 323 of 2002 renumbered as Title Suit No. 92 of 2003 upon its transfer to the Second Court of Assistant Judge, Dhaka.

2. The plaintiff filed the suit for certain declarations that the order of dismissal of the plaintiff is illegal, void and not binding upon the plaintiff and for reinstatement to all back wages and that the appointment of defendant No.4 on 7-1-2001 to be declared void, illegal, inoperative and prayed for an order of mandatory injunction stating, inter alia, that the appellant was appointed as an External Affairs Officer of the office of the World Bank, Dhaka through a rigorous selection process for 2 years as a probationer with effect from 16 January 2000. The appellant rendered excellent service, recognised as well by the World Bank awarding her spot award salary increase and various compliments, both verbally and through e-mail. In spite of her successful discharge of duties, the appellant all on a sudden on 3rd May 2001 was served with a notification that she would not be confirmed and her employment with the defendant World Bank would be terminated from 2nd July 2001. The appellant termed the termination as has been made without complying with the due process of law and in violation of the Bank's applicable rules and procedure and. in utter disregard and disrespect of the rules governing the staffs embodied in the Staff Manual embodying the terms and conditions of the service of the employees including the appellant.

3. Upon service of notice of the suit the defendant World Bank appeared in Court on 23-3-2002 but did not file any written statement whereupon the suit was fixed for hearing ex parte. When the defendant filed an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 23-3-2002 for rejection of the plaint. Meanwhile, despite an order of temporary injunction not to induct any staff to the post of the appellant, the defendant inducted one Subrata Dhar to the plaintiffs position with effect from January 1, 2002 in violation of the order of injunction. The appellant however, filed written objection against the application for rejection of plaint.

4. Upon hearing the same the learned Assistant Judge rejected the said application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The defendants, however, moved the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1476 of 2003 challenging the order dated 27-2-2003 and obtained a Rule and an order of stay of all further proceeding of Title Suit No. 92 of 2003. Upon contested hearing the High Court Division made the Rule absolute-in-part while affirming the order rejecting the application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure but directed the trial Court to first decide the question of maintainability of the suit under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act before recording of evidence, however, the High Court Division did not find that the suit is not maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

5. Thereafter, the appellant moved this Court and obtained the leave as under:

"Mr TH Khan, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner, submitted that the trial of a suit should not ordinarily be held piecemeal and the trial Court no longer has a discretion to avoid decisions on fact. It is now mandatory to try and determine the issues of fact along with the issues of law and the trial Court may hear the issue of maintainability as a preliminary issue but it must postpone its judgment until the suit is heard on all other issues and thereafter, it must give its findings on maintainability along with other issues. The main consideration underlying the general rule which deprecates piecemeal trial is in order to avoid a protracted litigation and unnecessary expenditure. The learned Counsel further submitted that the defendant-respondents did not file written statement in the trial Court and at this stage the trial Court has no opportunity to frame issue on the point of maintainability but the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division out of his misconceived idea about law and procedure of the trial Court illegally directed the trial Court to dispose of the question of maintainability before filing written  statement and taking evidence and, as such, the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is liable to be interfered with by this Court. The learned Counsel lastly, submitted that the Advocate of the defendants argued at the time of hearing of application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the trial Court, that the plaint is hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and so the plaint is liable to be rejected and that for repelling the said argument of the defendant's lawyer, the trial Court opined that the suit is not barred by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act but the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division made the Rule absolute in part, holding, inter alia, that the trial Court committed error of law by holding that the suit is not barred by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, that the above contention of the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division is misconceived and full of misreading of facts because of the fact that there is no reference in respect of rejection of the plaint under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and, as such, the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is liable to be interfered by this Court."

6. Mr TH Khan, the learned Counsel appearing for the appellant, submitted that it is now well settled that the trial. of a suit should not ordinarily be held piecemeal and the trial Court no longer has a discretion to avoid decisions on fact; as the trial under the circumstances is now mandatory and the Court is to determine the issues of fact along with the issues of law; the trial Court may, however, hear the issue of maintainability as it preliminary issue but must postpone its judgment until the suit is heard on all other issues and thereafter, it must give its findings on maintainability along with other issues; that the main consideration underlying the general rule which deprecates piecemeal trial is to avoid a protracted litigation and unnecessary expenditure and, in support of his submission, has referred to the decision in the case of Fazlur Rahman vs Rajab Ali and others reported in 30 DLR (SC) 30 wherein it has been held:

"It is of course the general rule of judicial procedure that the trial should not be held piecemeal so that the litigation may not be protected. Where the parties to a suit are at issue On several questions, all such questions should be heard together and disposed of by one judgment so that in case of reversal of the trial Court's decision on certain issues, there may not be any necessity for demand of the suit for the disposal of the undisposed of issues.

"The statutory mandate, as is contained in the above quoted rule, clearly directs that if the Court is of opinion that the suit or any part thereof may be disposed of on an issue of law only, it shall try that issue first even without settling the issues of fact. The whole object of this provision seems to be that if there is any issue of law on which the entire suit may be disposed of it is the duty of the Court to try that issue first at the earliest opportunity so that the Court may not be unnecessarily bogged down in a complicated trial of the issue of fact  requiring much time and involving heavy expenditure. The general principle is, no doubt, that the issues in a suit shall not be tried in parts but should be disposed of together. But the provision of Order XIV, rule 2 of the Code is a kind of exception to the said general rule. Under the said rule of Order XIV, after the filing of the written statement the Court may take up the hearing of an issue of law as a preliminary issue for decision if it' is of the opinion that the decision on such issue shall dispose of the entire suit or parts thereof, and may postpone even the settlement of issue of fact until the disposal of the' said issue of law. The compliance with this rule is particularly obligatory when the issue of law raises the question of jurisdiction of the Court to try the suit, as is in the present case."

7. In the cited decision though the trial of a suit in piecemeal has been discouraged but the general principle is that a suit or any part thereof may be disposed of by the Court on issue of law which should be tried first even without settling issue of fact and that the general principle of law that the issues in the suit should not be treated in part but disposed of together but the provision of Order XIV, rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure appears to be an exception to the said general rule under which after filing of the written statement the Court may take up for hearing an issue of law as preliminary issue for decision if it is of the opinion that the decision on issue of law as a preliminary one shall dispose of the entire suit or parts thereof and may postpone even the settlement of issues of fact until the disposal of the said issue of law. The compliance with this rule is particularly obligatory when the issue of law raises the question of jurisdiction of the Court to try the suit, as has been alleged by the respondent in the present case.

8. The learned Counsel further submitted that the defendant-respondents did not file written statement in the trial Court as yet and at this stage the trial Court is not in seizin of the facts constituting the pleading in the suit and yet has no opportunity to frame issue on the point of maintainability but the learned Judge of the High Court Division himself having failed to find that the suit, not maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act, out of misconceived idea about law and procedure, illegally directed the trial Court to dispose of the question of maintainability before filing of the written statement and taking evidence and, as such, the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is liable to be interfered with by this Court.

9. In the instant case admittedly the respondent has not yet flied any written statement detailing the facts and circumstances, for which allegedly the suit is not maintainable either under section 42 or 56F of the Specific Relief Act so as to avoid protracted litigation at an exorbitant cost. But the High Court Division considering the plaint only has directed the trial Court to decide the point of maintainability of the suit before recording of evidence.

<u>10. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, the learned Counsel appearing for the respondent Bank has, however, submitted that the suit flied against the defendant Bank is not maintainable under Article 7 of the Articles of Agreement contained in the International Financial Organisation Order 1972 (PO No. 86 of 1972) rendering the suit barred by law as the respondents enjoy privileges and immunities from legal process with respect to acts performed by them in their official capacity unless the same has been waived inasmuch as from averment the plaint itself gives rise to contract of appointment, the appellant has no character or legal right for the declaration and, as such, the suit is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. The learned Counsel has further submitted that the plaint as stood on amendment, the suit having been: filed for a mandatory injunction for reinstatement in service, is barred under section 56F of the Specific Relief Act   as where the contract is not specifically enforceable no injunction can be granted. The learned Counsel further submitted in view of the prayer for a declaration that the plaintiff is still in service and entitled to be reinstated with back wages is in executable in nature and the mandatory injunction as prayed for is barred under the law as spelt out in 7 MLR (AD) 4 that the suit is not per se maintainable. The learned Counsel has further submitted that the relationship between the plaintiff and the defendant being one of master and servant and an unwilling master cannot be trust upon with a servant by way of reinstatement through a decree in the suit.</u>

11. Mr TH Khan, the learned Counsel, has not disputed the proposition that the Court could reject a plaint considering the averments in the plaint itself where the suit as it stands is barred by any law but in the instant case that having not been done submitted that the defendant's plea in the instant case having failed in their attempt to reject the application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure the defendant could not at this stage apply for a modified plea of bar under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act which should ordinarily be decided on evidence on the facts to be disclosed in the pleading of the parties and has referred to a decision in the case of Guiness Peal (Trading) Limited vs Md Fazlur Rahman reported in 44 DLR (AD) 242 wherein it has been held that:

"When the Court rejects or refuses to reject a plaint it does so in exercise of its jurisdiction vested in it. Even where clause (d) is invoked on the ground that the suit is barred by law the Court is entitled to examine that question whether the defendant's plea is correct."

12. Mr TH Khan further submitted that the Court below concurrently found that the plaint is not liable to be rejected on the basis of the averments in the plaint as it stands today but once having considered the submissions of the learned Counsel for the petitioner as to whether the suit is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act detailing the decisions on the subject of the averment in the plaint itself but refrained from arriving at any finding on the question of maintainability holding the same to be an issue of law and that Order XIV, rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure authorises the Court to decide the issue of law instead of deciding the issue itself, acted illegally in directing the Court below to decide the issue as to maintainability before recording of the evidence.

13. The learned Counsel further submitted that the issue as to whether the suit was maintainable or not under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act cannot be decided on an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure as in the instant case the Courts below have concurrently found that the plaint is not liable to be rejected under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and that the maintainability of the suit can be determined at the time of trial and not under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the plaint cannot be rejected in limine under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure on the question of maintainability of the suit as has been held in the case of Sree Mukul Chandra Shah and others vs Babu Subash Chandra Sarker reported in 4 MLR (AD) 426.

14. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, the learned Counsel appearing for the respondents, has further submitted [Tom the relief in the plaint as amended in the suit being one for mandatory injunction for reinstatement of service is barred under section 56F of the Specific Relief Act and the suit is not maintainable as framed and has referred to a decision in the case of Rupali Bank Ltd vs Haji Md Arab Ali and others reported in 7 MLR (AD) 4.

<u>15. Admittedly, the suit in the reported decision arose out of the judgment and decree of the Courts below wherein the defendant filed written statement and led evidence and that the issue before the Court in the suit was as to the maintainability of the suit where the relationship between the Bank and the plaintiff employee was found to be that of master and servant and, as such, the question arose as to whether they are entitled to the relief claimed for. The said decision has held, inter alia, that:</u>

<u>"In view of the legal position as discussed above, we need not decide the issue as to whether the dismissal from service in question was illegal, but we must hold that the suit is not maintainable on the ground that a declaratory decree will not be enough and that a decree for mandatory injunction necessary as a consequential relief is barred under the law. We, therefore, find that neither the trial Court nor the appellate Court nor the High Court Division considered this vital issue which cuts at the root resulting that the suit is not maintainable as framed. The suit ought to have been dismissed on the issue."</u>

16. In the instant case, the defendant-respondent has framed certain Service rules/regulations in order to regulate the terms and conditions of the service of the plaintiff and it is to be decided on materials on record as to whether the said principles are applicable in the instant case upon averments in the written statement to that effect and evidence to be led on the pleading and thus, it will not be proper at this stage reading the plaint itself in the absence of any other materials on record to follow the said decision to hold that the suit as framed is not maintainable.

17. Similar is the case regarding the respondents allegation regarding the averment in the plaint in paragraph 5 of the plaint wherein the plaintiff has stated that she challenged the self same impugned action as disclosed in the plaint before the appellate Tribunal of the World Bank defendant No. 1. The respondent has added an issue by stating that whereupon the plaintiff received US$ 38,816.75 as compensation, etc on 27-6-2003 from the defendant Administrative Tribunal in Washington thereby rendering the present suit as wastage of public time and money, the plaint ought to have been rejected under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure in respect of the same cause of action being the subject-matter of the suit which is being barred by law and has also referred to a decision in the cases of 53 DLR (AD) 12 and 51 DLR (AD) 221. Both these decisions referred to are the products of protected litigations and final adjudication of the suit wherein written statement was filed and the suit have been disposed of on evidence, but in the instant case there is nothing on record of the suit except the plaint itself and both the Courts below found that the plaint is not liable to be rejected but the High Court Division has remanded the suit to the trial Court for decision on considering the same as to maintainability itself to be found as to whether the plaint as stands today, as to whether the suit is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act or not.

<u>18. The learned Counsel for the respondent has submitted regarding the immunity of the respondent to be sued in our Courts, for which the suit is not maintainable. The question of immunity is a mixed questions of law and facts and the material has to be produced by way of averments in the written statement and thereafter the materials are required to be considered in the light of the evidence in the suit and a decision should be arrived at accordingly.</u>

19. Mr Huq has finally submitted that in the absence of any appeal preferred by the respondent this Court could take resort to Order XLI, rule 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure which enables the respondent to seek a relief even without filing an appeal or cross-objection and that relief also could be given beyond the leave order for ends of justice and in order to do complete justice by rejecting the plaint on the ground that the suit is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and has referred to a decision in the case of Mst Shamim Akhtar vs Syed A/am Hussain and others reported 1975 SCMR 60 wherein it has been held that:

"The rule is at best a rule of practice only developed as a result of the practice of the Judicial Committee and, therefore, like all rules of practice it can legitimately be departed from if the interests of justice so demand. The Judicial Committee itself adopted this principle in the case of Bibhabati vs Ramendra Narayan (AIR 1947 PC 19) and departed from an equally firmly established rule that it will not in civil matters interfere with a concurrent finding of fact. This Court also did the same thing in the case of Federation of Pakistan vs Ali Hasan (PLD 1967 SC 249)".

<u>20. We do not dispute the proposition of law but in the facts and circumstances of the case since the Courts below have not found the plaint liable to be rejected for good reasons assigned, we are not inclined to take resort to the said principle of law in order to obviate the necessity of filing an appeal by the respondent or to invoke our plenary jurisdiction for doing a complete justice.</u>

<u>21. In view of our discussion above, we are of the view that the issues of law impliedly arose therefrom as to whether the suit is barred under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act read with section 56F of the Specific Relief Act could be conveniently decided by the trial Court upon the filing of the written statement containing certain material averments on behalf of the defendant which are vital for consideration of the issues as to maintainability and evidence is required to be led in support thereof. Ends of justice would best be served if we confined ourselves to the leave granting order instead of exercising our power under Article 104 of the Constitution and allowing the respondents to take resort of Order XLI, rule 33 of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

In the result, the appeal is dismissed with modification of the order of the High Court Division and the trial Court is hereby directed to hear the suit on all issues including the issue regarding maintainability in accordance with law.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party Nos. 1, 3 and 4 to show cause as to why the impugned Judgment and decree dated 20-5-1996, decree signed on 26-5-1996 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Feni, in Title Appeal No. 22 of 1988 affirming the judgment and decree dated 29-12-1987, decree signed on 28-2-1988 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Dagonbhuiyan, Feni, in Title Suit No. 91 of 1977 renumbered as Title Suit No. 52 of 1986 dismissing the suit should not be set aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Facts leading to the issuance of this Rule, in short, are that the plaintiff-petitioner instituted the Title Suit No. 91 of 1977 in the Court of the Munsif, 2nd Court, Feni praying for partition of his share upon determination of title, stating, inter alia, that the defendant No. 1 sold out 60 decimals of land to him on 25-12-1972 under a registered suf kabala in which the plaintiff had enjoyment of his right, title and interest. The defendant No.3 gave him possession in Plot No. 1701 for 50 decimals and another 10 decimals in Plot No. 1495. After about two years of that sale, the defendant No. 1 tried to buy back the said land from the plaintiff and since the plaintiff did not agree to that the defendant, in connivance with his family members and also taking the advantage of not having any previous partition, tried to evict him from the suit land, lastly em 9-6-1977 and thus he was obliged to institute the suit.

3. The defendant Nos. 2 and 3 by filing a joint written statement contested suit stating that the defendant Nos. 1 to 3 got the suit property by way of inheritance and they were in enjoyment of their right, title and possession of the same. The defendant Nos. 1 to 3 by acceptance of part payment of Taka 3,500 from one Mohammad Miah out of consideration money of Taka 4,000 executed a Bainapatra for sale for 81 decimals of land on 3 -1 0- 1971 and handed over its possession to him on that day where the said Mohammad Miah is in enjoyment of the right, title and possession, It was agreed that the sale deed will be executed within the month of Baishakh, 1382 Bangla which they could not do and as such, Mohammad Miah instituted a suit in the year 1975 for Specific Performance of Contract. The defendant had no saleable interest in the suit land after the sale agreement with Mohammad Miah.

4. The learned trial Court was pleased to frame the following issues:

(i) Whether the suit was maintainable in its form;

(ii) Whether the suit is filed on proper valuation;

(iii) Whether the suit is bad for defect of parties;

(iv) Whether the suit is bad for hotch potch;

(v) Whether the plaintiff was entitled to get any decree as he prayed for;

(vi) Whether plaintiff was entitled to get any other relief.

5. The learned trial Court after taking evidence was pleased to dismiss the suit holding that the suit was not maintainable in its form and the plaintiff was not entitled to the relief he prayed for.

6. The plaintiff has thereafter preferred the Title Appeal No. 121 of 1983 before the Court of the District Judge, Feni and by his judgment and decree dated 21-6-1986 the learned District Judge was pleased to allow the appeal on his findings that "the learned Munsif did not frame any issue about the right, title, interest and possession of the parties in the suit land and the learned Munsif did not record any finding about the right, title and interest of any parties in the suit land."

7. The learned District Judge has thereafter sent the case back on remand directing the learned trial Court "to frame an issue in the suit about the right, title, interest and possession of the plaintiff in the suit land and record a specific finding. It has also directed the learned lower Court to record specific findings about the title of the parties after assessing the evidence on both sides." The learned appellate Court has also given an option to the plaintiff to amend the plaint seeking specific relief about the unregistered Bainapatra by which the defendant No. 4 claims title in the suit property.

8. On receipt of the suit back on remand the learned Assistant Judge, Dagonbhuiyan, Feni, renumbered it as Title Suit No. 52 of 1986 and framed the following issues:

(i) Whether the suit was maintainable in its form;

(ii) Whether there was any cause of action for filing the suit

(iii) Whether the suit was barred by limitation;

(iv) Whether the plaintiff had right, title and possession in the suit land;

(v) Whether the plaintiff was entitled to a decree;

(vi) Whether plaintiff was entitled to any other relief.

9. Upon conclusion of the evidence and hearing thereof the learned Assistant Judge was again pleased to dismiss the suit holding that the plaintiff by virtue of his purchase deed i.e. the Exhibit 1, did not obtain the possession of the suit hind and the defendant No.4 proved his possession in the suit land and that since the defendant No.4 is in possession of the suit land, his Bainapatra i.e. exhibit A was a valid and genuine instrument and that the sale deed of the plaintiff, i.e. the Exhibit 1, was a collusive instrument and, as such, it was neither effective nor acted upon. Since the plaintiff had no right, title and possession in the suit land he had no cause of action for filing the suit.

10. The plaintiff has again preferred an appeal being the Title Appeal No. 22 of 1998 which was ultimately heard and disposed of by the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), 1st Court, Feni, who by his judgment and decree dated 20-5-1996 disallowed the appeal affirming the judgment and decree of the trial Court holding that the defendant No. 1 has executed the sale deed in favour of the plaintiff on 25-12-1972, but prior to that he executed the Bainapatra in question on 10-3-1971 in respect of the same land and in favour of the defendant No. 4 and since the defendant No. 4 proved his possession in the suit land by adducing evidence on the basis of the Bainanama, from 3-10- 1971 and thereafter, also obtained a suf-kabala in a suit for Specific Performance of Contract, the defendant No. 1 had no subsisting right in the suit land to transfer to the plaintiff on 25-12-1972 and, as such, the sale deed i.e. exhibit 1, is ineffective and the plaintiff has acquired no right, title and possession in the suit land by virtue of the said sale deed.

11. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned Appellate Court disallowing the appeal and affirming those of the trial Court, the plaintiff appellant has preferred this application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the instant Rule.

12. Mr Md Nurul Mostafa, the Learned Advocate, appearing for the petitioner, has, after placing the judgments and decrees of the Courts below and the evidence adduced by the parties, submits that both the Courts below did not comply with the directives given by the learned first Appellate Court at the time of remanding the Title Suit No. 91 of 1977 back for re-trial on specific direction to find out right, title and possession of the parties in the suit land together with finding out the legal position of toe Bainapatra on the face of the registered sale deed.

13. The learned Advocate further argued that the learned trial Court with a view to find out right, title and possession of the suit land has banked only upon the possession leaving aside all other factors, and the learned Appellate Court has mechanically affirmed the said finding of the trial Court.

14. Mr Mohammad Ali Azzam, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party Nos. 1 to 3, submits, on the other hand, that the Court below have ascertained the right, title and possession of the parties in the suit land and together with the validity of the instruments, namely, the Bainapatra and the sale deed in compliance with the directions given by the first Appellate Court. He further submits that the instant suit was filed after disposal of the suit filed by the defendant No.4 praying for a decree for specific performance of contract. But the plaintiff, knowing fully well about the proceedings of that suit; did not implead himself as a party in that suit. The suit was decreed on 22-1-1976, the sale deed was executed through the Court on 19-11-1977 and the instant suit was instituted on 15-6-1977.

15. The learned Advocate then argued that after execution of the Bainapatra and transfer of possession in favour of the defendant No.4 by the defendant No.1, the defendant No. 1 had no subsisting interest in the suit land to transfer to the plaintiff. From the evidence on record it is proved that the defendant No.4 is in possession of the suit land to the knowledge of the plaintiff and the plaintiff is fully aware of the transaction between the defendant Nos. 1 and 4, before his purchase. The learned Courts below have rightly held that the plaintiff was not entitled to any relief in the given facts and circumstances of the suit.

16. Mr Nurul Mostafa, the learned Advocate, has, on the other hand, argued that from the evidence on record it cannot be said that the Plaintiff was aware of the transaction between the defendant No. 1 and the defendant No.4. The plaintiff was a bonafide purchaser without notice and his sale deed will have the preference over the Bainapatra.

17. The Bainapatra was a forged and collusive one, inasmuch as the means of payment of part performance is concerned. The currency notes that the PWs mentioned to have been used for payment, were handed at the relevant time.

<u>18. In support of his contention Mr Nurul Mostafa has relied upon the case of Pordil Khan vs Sufaid Gul and others, reported in 1965 P LD (Peshawar) 259.</u>

<u>19. Mr Mohammad Ali Azzam, on the other hand, has placed his reliance upon the case of Rupe Jahan Begum and others vs Lutfe Ali Chowdhury and others, reported in 49 DLR (AD) 73 submitting that the concurrent findings of the Courts below may not be disturbed by this Court in revision unless they are perverse in law.</u>

<u>20. In the case of Sudhir Chandra Shuklabadhya vs Amulya Shuklabadhya and others (unreported) this Bench had placed its reliance upon the case of Pordi! Khan vs Sufaid Gul and others, reported in PLD 1965 (Peshawar) 259, where, in similar circumstances; their Lordships held that "Where the previous sale of land was by an unregistered deed and possession was not delivered in consequence thereof and subsequently, the same land was sold to another person by a registered deed the subsequent sale has precedence over the previous sale."</u>

<u>But the cardinal' point in this reported case is the possession which is a condition-precedent for application of the Rule.</u>

<u>21. In the said unreported case this Bench had also placed its reliance upon the case of Magu Barma vs Bholi Dass and others, reported in AIR 1914 Cat 331 where their Lordships held that "the onus of showing that the subsequent registered transferee had notice of the prior unregistered document is on the person alleging it."</u>

22. In the instant case, both the Courts below on assessment of evidence on record found that the defendant No.4 was in possession of the suit land from the date of execution of the Bainapatra and that by adducing sufficient evidence the defendants proved notice of the plaintiff about the prior unregistered sale and, as such, the principles relied upon in the unreported case of Sudhir Chandra Shuklabadhya vs Amulya Shuklabadhya and others are distinguishable from the instant case.

<u>23. On perusal of the Judgments of the Courts below it cannot be said that the learned trial Court or, for that matter, the appellate Court did not comply with the directives given by the first Appellate Court, at the time of making remand, on the availability of evidence on record in that respect. Since the Courts below found that the plaintiff was aware of previous transaction i.e. the execution of Bainapatra and delivery of possession of the suit land in accordance with the Bainapatra, I do not find any merit in this Rule.</u>

24. The question of currency used for part performance was whether banned or not at the relevant time, is a peripheral matter and not of much help in reversing the concurrent findings of the Courts below.

25. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The impugned Judgment and decree dated 20-5-1996, decree signed on 26-5- 1996 passed by the learned Subordinate Judgeless Court, Feni, in Title Appeal No. 22 of 1988 affirming the judgment and decree dated 29-12- 1987, decree signed on 28-2-1988 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Dagonbhuiyan, Feni, in Title Suit No. 91 of 1977 renumbered as Title Suit No. 52 of 1986 is hereby upheld.

Send down the Lower Courts' records at once.

End.
