parties:
Titas Gas Transmission and Distribution Co Ltd ----- Appellant
Vs.
Shams Company and others ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
This appeal was on 3-12-1990 presented by the defendant No. 1 against judgment and decree dated 4-9-1990 passed by Subordinate Judge at Brahmanbaria in Title Suit No. 35 of 1986.

2. Facts are not disputed. Respondent No. 1 as plaintiff on 21-5-1986 instituted the suit in the Court of the Subordinate Judge at Brahmanbaria for a decree, declaring the right and title of the plaintiff in the suit land;

a.	declaring the use and occupation of the suit land by defendant No. 1 is illegal, unauthorised and malafide;

b.	defendant No. 1 is not entitled to own the suit land under provisions of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Act, 1982 until it has restored the vacant possession of the suit land to the plaintiff; and

c.	 the defendant No. 1 is not legally or ethically entitled to encash the Guarantee No. 14/01 dated 30-3-1985 issued by the defendant No.7, the Manager, Rupali Bank, Brahmanbaria Branch, Brahmanbaria until it pays the proper and lawful value with compensation and interest for its illegal use and occupation of the suit land till date.

3. Defendant No. 1 appeared and resisted the suit by filing a written statement denying plaint case. Defendant Nos. 2 to 6 also filed a joint written statement. In their joint written statement, it is mainly stated that average valuation of the land would be 12,00,000 per acre as per the valuation of the Brahmanbaria Sub-Registry and that was informed to the defendant No. 1 by the Deputy Commissioner at Brahmanbaria by his memo No. 271/1(1)/LA dated 15-10-1985.

4. Then, on 2-5-1990 both the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 made a joint application for referring all the matters involved in the suit to arbitration. They also agreed to appoint Mr M A Karim, a Senior Advocate and the President of the High Court Bar Association at Comilla. On hearing the application and being of the view that no substantive relief was sought for against any other defendants, the learned Subordinate Judge referred the dispute in between the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 of the suit to arbitrator, Mr M A Karim as agreed for making an award by his order dated 12-5-1990. On 6-8-1990 the learned Arbitrator gave the award to the following effect,

a.	the plaintiff has got right, title and interest in 0.5280 acre of land equivalent to 23,000 square feet as described in schedule C to the plaint;

b.	the defendant No. 1 is trespasser in the suit land;

c.	the plaintiff is entitled to a decree for Taka 43 (forty-three) lac only as value of the suit land and compensation for his loss of business or earnings from the year 1982 to December, 1989 and interest on this amount at the rate of 12% which the defendant No. 1 is liable to pay within a period as per direction of the Court; and

d.	 the plaintiff is directed to execute and register a kabala in favour of defendant No. 1 without any consideration within 15 days of the decree at the cost of defendant No.1 in respect of 0.5280 acre of land out of schedule C to the plaint excepting plot No. 1452.

5. On 8-8-1990 the award was filed in Court and the Court directed to put up the same on 8-9-1990. The plaintiff on 11-8-1990 made an application for acceptance of the award. Hearing the application, the Court fixed the matter for order on the date fixed earlier. The plaintiff again on 3-9-1990 made an application for passing the order on the very same date. On behalf of the defendant No. 1 copy of the application was received without any objection. The learned Subordinate Judge allowed application as there was no objection on behalf of the defendant No.1 and directed the office to put up the matter on 4-9-1990 for order.

6. On 4-9-1990 at about 5-00 PM the matter was taken up for order. Learned Subordinate Judge accepted the award as he found no objection raised either by the plaintiff or defendant No. 1 against the same. He also directed that the defendant No. 1 is liable to pay interest at the rate mentioned in the award till realisation. Plaintiff was directed to execute and register a kabala in favour of the defendant No.1 in respect of 0.5280 acre of land out of schedule C to the plaint excepting plot No. 1452 within 20 days from the date of decree at the cost of the defendant No.1. Decree was according, drawn, signed and sealed.

7. On 5-6-1991 this Division admitted the appeal for hearing. On the objections raised on behalf of the plaintiff against admission that in view of the provisions of section 39 of the Arbitration Act, briefly the Act, the appeal was not maintainable, this Division however directed the DAG (Civil) to assist the Court at the time of hearing of the appeal.

8. In support of the appeal Mrs Sufia mainly submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge erred in law in passing the judgment without giving any opportunity to the defendant No. 1 for filing objections against the award. Mr Habibul Islam Bhuiyan opposed her on two counts. Firstly he submitted that the appeal was not maintainable under section 39 of the Arbitration Act. Secondly, he submitted that after the judgment and decree, the plaintiff wrote to the defendant No. 1 for taking steps for execution and registration of the kabala, and the plaintiff had to execute and register the kabala in favour of the defendant No.1 within their knowledge as per direction in the judgment. He also drew my attention to the fact that the reference was made jointly by the plaintiff and defendant No. 1, that the award that was filed in Court was also jointly signed by both plaintiff and defendant No.1, and that the defendant No. 1 never ever raised any objection at any point of time to any order as passed by the trial Court and/or the award as given by the arbitrator. After 11 years, such technical question cannot be allowed to come in the way of justice.

9. In reply, Mrs Sufia submitted that defendant No. 1 had never asked the plaintiff to execute and register the kabala. Defendant No. 1 had no hand to whatever the plaintiff did and therefore, the defendant No.1's appeal cannot fail on legal ground.

10. Mr Abdul Quayum, learned Deputy Attorney-General submitted that even if the appeal was found to be not maintainable the memorandum of appeal could be converted into a revision application. In support, he cited the decision in the case of Bangladesh Water Development Board and others vs Progati Prakaushali and another 49 DLR 335. In the case, the appeal presented against an order passed under section 17 of the Arbitration Act was found to be not maintainable and the memorandum of the appeal was converted by a Division Bench of this Division into a revision in the interest of justice, and the same was accordingly disposed of.

11. In order to appreciate the rival contentions, I should refer to the relevant law, which are sections 14, 17, 21 and 39 of the Arbitration Act that read as under,

14. (1) When the arbitrators or umpire have made their award they shall sign it and. shall give notice in writing to the parties of the making and signing thereof

(2) The arbitrators or umpire shall.........cause the award or a signed copy of it, together with any depositions and documents which may have been taken and proved before them to be filed in Court, and the Court shall thereupon give notice to the parties of the filing of the award.

(3) 	.

17. Where the Court sees no cause to remit the award or any of the matters referred to arbitration for consideration or to set aside the award, the Court shall, after the time for making an application to set aside the award has expired or such application having been made. after refusing it, proceed to pronounce judgment according to the award, and upon the judgment so pronounced a decree shall follow, and no appeal shall lie from such decree except on the ground' that it is in excess, of, or not otherwise in accordance with, the award.

21. Where in any suit all the parties interested agree that any matter in difference between them in the suit shall be referred to arbitration, they may at any time before judgment is pronounced apply in writing to the Court for an order of reference.

22. The arbitrator shall be appointed in such manner as may be agreed upon between the parties.

23. (1) The Court shall, by order, refer to the arbitrator the matter in difference which he is required to determine, and shall in the order specify such time as it thinks reasonable for the making of the award.

(2) Where a matter is referred to arbitration, the Court shall not, save in the manner and to the extent provided in this Act, deal with such matter in the suit.

39. (1) An appeal shall lie from the following orders passed under this Act (and from no others) to the Court authorised by law to hear appeals from original decrees of the Court passing the order:

An order-

i. 	superseding an arbitration;

ii. on an award stated in the form of a special case;

iii.   modifying or correcting an award;

iv. 	filing or refusing to file an arbitration agreement;

v. staying or refusing to stay legal proceedings where there is an arbitration agreement;

vi. 	setting aside or refusing to set aside an award.

Provided that the provisions of this section shall not apply to any order passed by a Small Cause Court.

(2) No second appeal shall lie from an order passed in appeal under this section, but nothing in this section shall affect or take away any right to appeal to the Supreme Court.

12. In view of above provisions, it may be stated-

Under sections 21 to 23 of the Act, when the parties interested agree and apply for referring their difference in the suit to an agreed arbitrator at any time before the pronouncement of judgment, the Court is obliged to refer the matter in difference to the arbitrator and it shall specify in the order the time for making the award. After award was given, that must be filed in Court under section 14 and the Court is obliged thereupon to serve notice upon the parties of the filing of the award. Then, under section 17, if the Court finds no reason to remit the award or any matter in difference back to the arbitrator for reconsideration or does not set aside the award, the Court shall pronounce judgment but only after the expiration of the time for making an application to set aside the award or refusing the application if any made. Article 158 of the Limitation Act has provided a period of 30 days from the service of notice of filing of the award for making an application to set aside an award. A decree thereupon shall follow such judgment. But no appeal shall lie against such decree on the ground that the decree is in excess of or not exactly in accordance with the award. Under section 39, the orders against which an appeal shall lie have been enumerated.

13. In the case before me, it is not disputed that the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 are only parties interested in the suit. They jointly made an application for referring the disputes as raised in the suit to an agreed arbitrator. In view of the above provisions of sections 21 to 23 of the Act, the Court referred the matter in difference to said arbitrator. On 6-8-1990 the arbitrator made the award. On 8-8-1990 the award was filed in Court. Thereupon, the Court fixed 8-9-1990 for order on the award. But on an application dated 3-9-1990 of the plaintiff, the Court fixed 4-9-1990 for order on the award, and on 4-9-1990 the Court pronounced the judgment ex parte i.e. in the absence of the appellant, whereupon the decree followed. It appears from the record that the judgment was shown on 5-9-1990, the following day of pronouncement of judgment to the learned Advocates of both parties.

<u>14. Record shows that after receipt of the award on 8-8-1990, no notice was issued and/or served by the Court upon the parties of the filing of the award. Moreover, the Court pronounced the judgment before the expiration of the period for making an application to set aside the award as stated earlier. Section 17 of the Act however does not require of the Court to give any date for filing any objection to the award. If a party wants an award to be set aside on any of the grounds mentioned in section 30 of the Act, it must apply within 30 days of the date of service of notice of filing of the award as provided in article 158 of the Limitation Act. Pronouncing of the judgment under section 17 is made subject to the expiration of the period of 30 days from the date of service of the notice of filing of the award and this is a condition precedent to the exercise of the jurisdiction by the Court under the section.</u>

15. In the case of Secretary to the Government of Karnaka vs Harishbabu, (1996) 5 SCC 400, leave was granted by the Supreme Court of India to consider when does the period of imitation commence for filing objections seeking setting aside of an arbitration award. In the case, there is answer to all questions raised in this appeal. The Supreme Court of India held in para 15,

"In view of the settled law and our discussion above, our answer to the question posed in the opening part of the judgment is that the period of the limitation for filing objections seeking the setting aside of an arbitration award commences from the date of service of the notice issued by the Court upon the parties regarding the filing of the award under section 14 (2) of the Act. Such a notice need not be in writing but what is essential is that the notice or intimation or communication of the filing of the award must be issued by the Court to the parties and served upon the parties concerned. Date of service of a notice issued by the arbitrator under section 14(1) of the Act or the date of obtaining an endorsement on the award by the arbitrator from the party concerned is irrelevant for determining the question of limitation for filing objections under Article 119 (b) of the Limitation Act, 1963 (Article 158 of Limitation Act, 1908)."

16. Now what is the remedy from such ex parte decree? It is also now settled that in view of section 41 of the Act, all the remedies as are available against such ex parte decree under the Code of Civil Procedure is equally available subject however to the provisions of the Act. Second part of section 17 says, "no appeal shall lie from such decree except on the ground that it is in excess, of, or not otherwise in accordance with, the award". The scope of an appeal provided from the decree appears to be limited. The appeal is available only when the decree is in excess of the award or not exactly in accordance with the award. So, the appeal provided by section 17 is completely different from that available under section 39 of the Act. Under section 39, the orders have been enumerated from which an appeal shall lie. Under section 17, when an order is passed in setting aside the award or in refusing to set aside the award, an appeal shall lie under clause vi of section 39 (1).

<u>17. In my view, as discussed above the learned Subordinate Judge, without following the mandatory provisions of section 14 of the Act fell in serious error of law in pronouncing the judgment. The decree followed such judgment must be held to be clearly in excess of the award. The appeal from such decree is therefore, quite competent and must succeed.</u>

18. In the result, this appeal is allowed. The parties are directed to bear their own costs. The impugned judgment and decree dated 4-9-1990 are set aside. The case is sent back on remand to the trial Court for fresh disposal of the suit in accordance with law after taking into consideration of the objections to be filed by the appellant for setting aside the award. Since the suit is pending for a long time, I grant 30 days time to the appellant for filing the objections before the trial Court, and the trial Court is directed to dispose of the suit expeditiously after giving opportunity of hearing to both parties and as soon as within six months, from the date of receipt of the records.

Send down the records at once.

End.

parties:
Hazera Begum ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Artha Rin Adalat & another ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Hamidul Haque J: This Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 20-7-2000 (Annexure 'E') passed in Money Execution Case No. 2 of 1991 by the learned Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, Faridpur as far as it relates to the issuance of Civil Warrant of Arrest is concerned should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and to be of no legal effect.

2. We have found that in this Rule the petitioner is one of the judgment debtors in Artha Rin Adalat suit No. 2/91 of Artha Rin Adalat, Faridpur. The respondent No. 2, Agrani Bank is the plaintiff of that suit. The suit was decreed and decree holder filed an application for execution of the decree before the Artha Rin Adalat and from the order dated 16-7-97, we find that the execution case was disposed of on full satisfaction but subsequently by the order dated 25-5-2000, the earlier order was vacated and the execution case continued. The decree holder then filed an application for passing an order for civil imprisonment of the judgment debtors. After hearing the parties, the court passed the impugned order on 20-7-2000, allowed the prayer of the decree holder and passed an order of issuing warrant of arrest for detention of the judgment debtor Nos. 2, 3 and 4. The judgment debtor No. 4 is the present petitioner before us.

3. Mr Sobhan along with Mr Abu Hena Razzaki appeared on behalf of the petitioner. Their main argument is that order of civil imprisonment of a woman is totally illegal. In this connection, they referred to section 56 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Mr Sobhan has also argued that no specific procedure has been laid down in the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 regarding execution of a decree. However, he conceded that the provisions relating to execution of a decree as laid down in the Code of Civil Procedure may not be applicable. According to him, as there is no specific procedure in the Artha Rin Adalat, there cannot be an order of civil imprisonment of a woman.

4. Mr MA Tariq appeared on behalf of the respondent decree holder. He has submitted that under section 6 Ka of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain 1990, the Artha Rin Adalat itself has been given the power to execute a decree passed by it. So, according to him, as the Artha Rin Adalat considered it fit and proper to pass an order for detention of the judgment debtors, the Adalat committed no illegality.

<u>5. We have perused the provisions of section 6 Ka regarding execution of a decree. The section is reproduce below:</u>

<u>"৬ক। ডিক্রি বাস্তবায়নে।-Code of Civil Procedure, 1908(Act V of 1908) এ যাহা কিছুই থাকুক না কেন কোন অর্থ ঋন আদালতের সিদ্ধান্ত উক্ত আদালত কর্তৃক জারী ও বাস্তবায়ন করা হইবে।"</u>

<u>The above section provides that notwithstanding anything contained in the Civil Procedure Code. Artha Rin Adalat may execute its decree. Under section 56 of the Code of Civil Procedure, civil Court cannot pass an order for detention in the civil imprisonment of a woman in execution of a decree for payment of money. In view of the language used in section 6 ka of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 the provisions of section 56 of the Code of Civil Procedure will not be a bar in passing an order for detention or arrest of a woman in execution of a decree for payment of money. So, we do not find that the Artha Rin Adalat committed any illegality in passing the impugned order of civil imprisonment of the petitioner.</u>

6. Mr Sobhan has pointed out that the provisions of section 6 ka are vague and, as such, there is scope of arbitrary exercise of power by Artha Rin Adalat. For proper appreciation of the legal position we may reproduce below the provisions of sub-sections (4) and (5) of section 5 of the Act:

"(৪) অর্থ ঋন আদালত একটি দেওয়ানী আদালত (Civil Court) বলিয়া গন্য হইবে এবং (Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Act V of 1908) এ দেওয়ানী আদালতের যে সমস্ত ক্ষমতা ও   এখতিয়ার আছে সেই সমস্ত ক্ষমতা ও এখতিয়ার, এই আইনের বিধান সাপেক্ষে অর্থঋন আদালতের ও থাকিবে।

(৫) এই আইনে ভিন্নরূপ কিছু না থাকিলে , অর্থঋন আদালত উহার কার্যক্রম পরিচালনার ব্যপারে (Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (Act V of 1908) এ দেওয়ানী  আদালতের কার্যক্রম পরিচালনার সম্পর্কে যে বিধান করা হইয়াছে উহা অনুসরণ করিবে।”

We cannot agree with Mr Sobhan if we peruse the provisions of section 6ka and the provisions of sub-sections (4) and (5) of section 5 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990.

<u>7. Under section 6 ka, the Artha Rin Adalat is empowered to execute its own decree but in executing such a decree, the provisions of the Code regarding execution of a decree shall not be binding upon the Adalat. In other words, if and when the Adalat considers it necessary, the Adalat may pass an order which may not be in conformity with the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure. In the instant case, though under section 56 of the Code of Civil Procedure there cannot be an order for detention or arrest of a woman for the purpose of realisation of money, the Artha Rin Adalat considered it fit and proper for the sake of realisation of money that the judgment debtors including the petitioner be detained in civil prisons. In view of the power given to such an Adalat under section 6 ka, the provisions of section 56 of the Code of Civil Procedure shall not be a bar for passing the above order.</u>

8. In addition to the provisions of section 6 ka, we find that under sub-section (4) of section 5, Artha Rin Adalat has been empowered to exercise all the powers of civil Court subject to the provisions of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain. Sub-section (5) of section 5 provides that the Artha Rin Adalat should follow the procedures laid down in the Code of Civil Procedure which are not inconsistent with the provision of the Act. Provisions not consistent with the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure have been included in some of the provisions of this Act, For example, under sub-section (2) of section 6, a defendant may file a case under Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure but in that case, the petitioner defendant shall have to deposit half of the decretal amount. This provision of the depositing half of the decretal amount is over and above the conditions laid down in Order 9 rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for filing a petition for setting aside an ex parte decree.

<u>9. From our above discussion, we have found that an Artha Rin Adalat constituted under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain 1990, shall follow the procedure laid down in the Code of Civil Procedure in discharging its function if there is nothing inconsistent in this Act itself. Under section 6 ka of the Act, the Adalat has been given power to pass an order which may not be in conformity with the provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure relating to execution of a decree. In view off this position, we find no illegality in the order passed by the Artha Rin Adalat. The Rule is liable to be discharged.</u>

In the result, the Rule is discharged. Stay granted earlier is vacated.

End.

full_judgment:
Siddiqur Rahman Miah J: This revisional application under section U5(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure at the instance of the plaintiff- appellant is directed against the judgment and decree dated 5-11-2003 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Court No.2, Rangpur, in Other Appeal No. 5 of 2003 dismissing the appeal and affirming those of the judgment and decree dated 24-9-2002 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Court No.1, Rangpur, in Other Suit No. 30 of 1997 decreeing the suit in part.

2. The petitioner as plaintiff filed other Suit No. 30 of 1997 in the Court of the learned Joint District Judge, Court No.1, Rangpur, praying for partition of an area of 4.70 acres of land out of the suit jote.

3. The plaintiff's case, in short, is that suit jote of schedule 'ka' originally belonged to Deyanat Ullah who died leaving behind his only son Delwar Sheikh; that suit jote of schedule 'Kha' belonged to plaintiff and Delwar Sheikh; that the suit jote of schedule 'Ga' and 'Gha' belonged to Maherunnessa, the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff and defendant No.1, that while they had been possessing the land of schedule 'Ka' and 'Kha', Delwar Sheikh died before SA record leaving behind wife Maherunnessa, one son, Nur Rahman, the defendant No.1 and one daughter Nurjahan, the plaintiff; that thereafter Maherunnessa died leaving behind only one son and one daughter, the defendant No. 1 and the plaintiff respectively. It is further contended that the plaintiff and the defendant No. 1 have been possessing the suit land in ejmali; that SA record of some khatians have been published correctly and some khatians have been published wrongly and collusively at the instance of the defendant No.1; that the plaintiff is entitled to get an area of 2.14 acres of land out of 'ka' schedule, an area of 2.06 acres of land out of 'kha' schedule, an area of 0.38 acres of land out of schedule 'ga' and an area of 0.12 acres of land out of schedule 'gha' of the suit jote and thereby the plaintiff has been possessing a grand total area of 4. 70 acres of land in ejmali out of the suit jote.

4. It is further set forth that Delwar Sheikh never transferred any land out of the suit jote in favour of the defendant No. 1 and if defendant No. 1 will show any such document of transfer, that will be forged and void document; that the plaintiff does not find it conducive to possess the suit land in ejmali and, therefore, she claimed partition of the suit jote on 10-11-1992 to which the defendant No. 1 denied and, as such, the plaintiff has been constrained to file the suit for partition.

5. The defendant Nos. 1, 16 and 18 also have contested the suit by filing joint written statement contending, inter alia, that the land of lot No.5 of schedule 'Ka' belonged 'to Deyanatullah whose father's name is Bhwa Sheikh; that Deyanatullah had given estafa of the land of lot No.5 of schedule 'ka' to the superior landlord who subsequently had sold out the same land in favour of defendant No. 1 vide registered deed dated 7-10-1952 and since then the defendant No. 1 has been possessing the same; that Deyanatullah transferred his rest land in favour of one Manazuddin by registered deed of sale dated 29-9-1955; that Minajuddin sold out an area of 0.15½ acres of land in favour of one Ashraful and an area of 0.15½ acres of land in favour of one Rafiqul and Golam Rabbani by registered deed of sale both dated 4-1-1978; that the land of lot Nos. 1 to 4 of schedule'ka' and 'Kha' belonged to Deyanatullah who died leaving behind his only son Delwar Sheikh; that the defendant No. 1 has purchased an area of 0.23 acres of land of schedule 'kha'; that Delwar Sheikh has transferred an area of 11.82 acres of land only out of schedule'ka' and 'kha' by an unregistered deed of Reba dated 19-6-1948 and thereafter he died leaving behind no properties; that the land of schedule 'ga' and 'gha' belonged to Maherunnessa, predecessor in interest of the plaintiff and defendant No.1, who has gifted out her entire properties orally in favour of the defendant No. land since then defendant No. 1 has been possessing the same.

6. It is further stated that the defendant No.1 has transferred an area of 2.68 acres of land out of the suit jote in favour of different persons and has been possessing the remaining lands; that the plaintiff has no right, title and interest over the suit land; that SA record of the suit jote are correct and that the plaintiff's suit is liable to be dismissed.

7. On the pleadings of the parties, the following issues were settled:

a)	Is the suit maintainable in its present form ?

b)	Is the suit properly valued and stamped?

c)	Is the suit bad for defect of parties?

d)	Is the unregistered Heba deed dated 19-6-1948 in respect of 'Ka' and 'Kha' schedule land genuine and whether the same is binding upon the plaintiff?

e)	Is the plaintiff owner in the suit land as per claim?

f)	Is the plaintiff entitled to get preliminary decree and other reliefs as prayed for ?

8. In support of her case, the plaintiff got 3 witnesses examined while defendant examined 5(five) witnesses. The papers and documents produced by the plaintiff are marked Exhibits 1 to 7, while those of the defendant are marked Exhibits "Ka' to 'Jha".

9. The plaintiff filed some documents in support of her contention. The plaintiff's power of attorney dated 17-9-1999 is Exhibit L certified copy of the CS khatians are Exhibits 2 to 2 (na), certified copy of the CS khatians Exhibits 3 to 3 (na), kabala dated 14-1-1941 is Exhibit 4, Kabala dated 7-12-1940 is Exhibit 5, Kabala dated 22-4-1943 and Kabala dated 14-7-1943 are Exhibits 67 while the defendant also filed some documents to prove his case. The CS khatians are marked Exhibits 'ka' to 'Ka(l), SA khatians are Exhibits 'Kha' to 'Kha(8), different kabalas are marked Exhibits 'Ga' to 'Ga(6), certified copies of judgment and decree of other Appeal No. 25 of 1995 is Exhibit 'Gha', certified copy Of deposition of witnesses in Other Suit No. 175 of 1992 are Exhibits Gha (7), Government rent receipts are Exhibits Uma to Uma(25), certified copy of the kabala deed dated 4-1-1978 is marked Exhibit Cha, certified copy of Kabala dated 7-10-1952 Is Exhibit Chha, certified copy of Kabala dated 29-4-1955 is marked Exhibit 'Ja' and unregistered deed dated 19-6-1948 is marked Exhibit 'jha'.

10. The suit was tried by the learned Joint District Judge, Court No.1, Rangpur, who upon hearing of both the parties and on perusal of the materials on record was pleased to decree the suit in part vide his-judgment and decree dated 24-9-2002.

11. Against the aforesaid judgment and decree dated 24-9-2002 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Court No.1, Rangpur, in Other Suit No. 30 of 1997, the plaintiff preferred an appeal being Other Appeal No. 5 of 2003 in the Court of the learned District Judge, Rangpur, which appeal on transfer was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, Court No.2, Rangpur, who upon hearing of both the parties and on perusal of the materials on record was pleased to dismiss the appeal affirming those of the judgment and decree appealed against vide his judgment and decree dated 5-11-2003.

12. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied-with the aforesaid judgment and decree dated 5-11-2003 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Court No.2, Rangpur, in Other Appeal No. 5 of 2003 dismissing the appeal and affimiing those of the judgment and decree dated 24-9-2002 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Court No.1, Rangpur, decreeing the suit in part. The plaintiff- appellant preferred this revisional application before this Court and obtained the present Rule.

13. Mr Rabi Shanker Chakraborty on behalf of Mr MA Latif Prodhan for the petitioner, submits that both the Courts below have committed an error of law in giving the status of an unregistered deed of gift dated 19-6-1948 into the status of a registered deed simply because of the fact that the deed is 30 years old without entering into the genuineness of the deed and that the learned Court below have committed an error of law resulting in an error in shifting the burden of proof of the genuineness of the unregistered deed of gift dated 19-6-1948 from the shoulder of the defendant onto the shoulder of the plaintiff. He further submits that the learned Court below have decided the suit on the basis of the findings given in Other Appeal No. 25 of 1995 which was decided only on some preliminary points but both the Courts below did not enter into the merit of the suit; that neither of the Courts below has given an independent findings and observations, while passing the impugned judgment and decree but reiterated the findings and observation given on preliminary points in Other Appeal No. 25 of 1995; that defendant No. 1 has failed to prove the genuineness of the nonjudicial stamp and the execution of the deed of gift dated 19-6-1948 and also failed to prove the fact as to why the said deed of gift was not registered and that both the Courts below have misread, misinterpreted and misconstrued the evidence and did not consider the material evidence on record while passing the impugned judgment and decree committing an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate refers the decision in the case of Sadek Ali vs Suruj All and others reported in 7 DLR 94 in support of his contention.

14. On the other hand, Mr Mahmudul Islam on behalf of Mr Md Shakawat Hossain for the defendant-opposite parties, submits that the unregistered deed of gift dated 19-6-1948 is genuine one through which the title of the suit land has been passed to defendant No. 1; that the plaintiff has failed to prove her case; that the learned Courts below considering the facts and circumstances of the case and evidence on record correctly passed the judgment and decree; that the learned Courts below did not misread, misinterpret and misconstrue the evidence and that the learned Courts below committed no illegality or material irregularity in passing the impugned judgment warranting any interference by this Court.

15. The only point for determination is, whether the learned Additional District Judge has committed an error of law resulting in an error in passing the impugned judgment and decree occasioning failure of justice.

16. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has placed before us the plaint and written statement, the deposition of the witnesses and documents filed by both the parties and the judgments of the appellate Court as well as of trial Court.

17. It is admitted that suit land belonged to Delwar Hossain and Maherunnessa who were father and mother of the plaintiff and defendant No. 1 respectively.

18. The plaintiff Nurjahan Begum filed the suit for partition for declaring the unregistered Heba deed dated 19-6-1948 executed by Delwar Sheikh false and collusive.

19. On the other hand, the defendant No.1 has claimed that his father Delwar Sheikh transferred the land of schedule 'ka' and 'Kha' measuring 11.82 acres of land by an unregistered Heba deed dated 19-6-1948 and his mother Maherunness also transferred 'Ga' and 'Gha' schedule land on 15-12-1973 by oral gift in his favour; that he transferred 2.68 acres of land to Abdur Rahim, Abdul Hakim, Abdul Sattar, Rahima, Rabiul, Anowar, Hamidul and Razzaqul Haider and he has been possessing the rest land mutating his name and paying rent to the government.

20. The pertinent question that calls for our determination is, whether the unregistered Heba deed dated 19-6-1948 and oral gift dated 15-12-1973 are genuine and whether any title has been passed to defendant No. 1 by virtue of such deeds. Both the Courts concurrently found the unregistered Heba deed dated 19-6-1948 as genuine and the oral gift dated 15-12-1973 not genuine.

21. On perusal of the evidence on record it appears that being inconvenienced in possession , the plaintiff, Nurjahan Begum, filed Partition Suit No. 175 of 1992 in which the defendant No.1 filed written statement claiming 11.82 acres of land by virtue of unregistered Heba deed dated 19-6-1948 and claiming the land of his mother, Maherunnessa, by virtue of oral gift, Suit No. 175 of 1992 was decreed ex parte on 30-1-1995. Being aggrieved by the decree, the defendant No.1, Nur Rahman, preferred Other Appeal No. 25 of 1995 which was allowed with the finding that the suit is undervalued and is out of pecuniary jurisdiction and that the suit is bad for defect of parties and that further decided permitting the plaintiff to file a fresh suit. As regard the un-registered deed dated 19-6-1948, the appellate Court opined that the plaintiff is the elder sister of the defendant No. 1; that the plaintiff was given many moveable and immovable properties at the time of her marriage, that the plaintiff did not file the suit which was actually filed forging ammuktemama, that the defendant No. 1 was permitted to impound the unregistered Heba deed. The appellate Court found the unregistered Heba deed dated 19-6-1948 genuine and treating the oral gift as not genuine. As per the direction of the, earlier appellate Court, the present suit being No. 30 of 1997 was filed which was decreed with the finding that the unregistered Heba deed dated 19-6-1948 is genuine one and oral gift dated 15-12-1973 is not genuine. On appeal, the appeal being No. 5 of 2003, was dismissed affirming the judgment of the trial Court.

22. In this suit, the plaintiff examined 3 PWs, while the defendant No.1 examined 5 DWs in support of their respective contentions. The plaintiff produced documents marked Exhibit 1 to 7, while the documents of the defendant No.1 were marked Exhibits Ka to Jha.

23. Law regarding burden of proof is envisaged in section 101 of the Evidence Act, wherein it is stated that the burden of proof lies on the party who substantially asserts the affirmative of the issue and not upon the party who denies it. Moreover, it is reasonable and just that the suitor who relies upon the existence of a fact, should be called upon to prove his own case. The party on whom the onus of proof lies must, in order to succeed, establish a prima facie case. He cannot on failure to do so, take advantage of the weakness of his adversary's case. He must succeed by the strength of his own right and clearness of his own proof.

24. Thus, the plaintiff Nurjahat Begum herself neither filed Title Suit No. 175 of 1992 nor filed the present Title Suit No. 30 of 1997. Both suits were filed by an Ammukter. The contention of the defendant No.1 is, that the said Ammukternama is a forged one. The plaintiff has relinquished her claim of the suit property as she got other moveable and immovable property. There is substance in the contention of the defendant No.1.

25. PW 1 Anowarul Islam, is the son of the plaintiff, who deposed that he is not party in the suit. He denied the suggestion to the effect that his mother did not come to the Court to depose as she relinquished the property getting other moveable and immovable property.

26. PW 2, Md Shamser Ali, deposed that he borga cultivated the suit land but he cannot say the area of the suit land nor can he say the plot number under his cultivation. He further deposed that plaintiff and defendant No. 1 ejmali possess the suit land and defendant No.1, Nur Rahman, gives crop to the plaintiff. There are some contradictions in his evidence. PW 3, Ahmed Ali, deposed that defendant No. 1 possesses the suit land and used to give half of the crops to the plaintiff. Thus, we find serious contradictions in the evidence of PWs as regard possession of the plaintiff in the suit land and all the PWs remain silent as to the genuineness of the unregistered Heba deed dated 19-6-1948.

27. On the other hand, SA record in respect of the major portion of the suit land is in the name of the defendant No.1, Nur Rahman, on the basis of unregistered Heba deed and other deeds. The defendant No. 1 has filed SA records which are marked Exhibits Kha to Kha(8) and also filed 26 dakhilas which are marked Exhibits Uma to Uma (29). SA records and rent receipts manifestly indicate the prima facie possession of the defendant No.1. Though SA record and rent receipts are not the evidence of title but of possession which follows from legal title. We received support of our above view in the case of Abdul Kader Rari and others vs Kaiser Ahmed Howlader being dead his heirs Fatema Khatoon and others reported in 3 MLR 227. All these papers clearly support the possession of the defendant No.1. It further appears from record that the defendant No. 1 sold 2.65 acres of land to Abdur Rahim and 7 others who are also in possession of their respective land. Moreover, the defendant No. 1 adducing 5 witnesses has succeeded in proving his title on the basis of un- registered Heba deed dated 19-6-1948 and possession on the basis of such deed.

<u>28. It appears that the unregistered Heba deed was impounded under section 35 of the Stamp Act and it was taken into evidence under section 90 of the Evidence Act. The object of section 90 of the Evidence Act is that when a document is or purports to be more than thirty years old, if it be produced from what Court considers to be proper custody, it may be presumed (a) that the signature and every other part of such document, which purports to be in the handwriting of any particular person, is in that person's handwriting and (b) that it was duly executed and attested by the person by whom it purports to be executed and attested. Thirty years old document, produced from proper custody, not looking ex facie suspicious, presumption could be drawn in favour of the document. It is the general rule that an instrument thirty years old proves itself, provided it be produced from a proper custody, then there is no necessity for further proof. We find support of the above view in the case of Parkash Chand vs Hans Raj, AIR 1994 HP 144.</u>

29. In view of the above law and evidence, we are of the view that the unregistered Hebanama dated 19-6-1948 appears to be genuine.

<u>30. The claim of the defendant No; 1 as regard schedule 'ka' and 'kha' that he acquired the same from his mother Maherunnessa by virtue of oral gift dated 15-12-1973 has not been substantiated. The learned appellate Court in Appeal No. 25 of 1995 held that the oral gift dated 15-12-1973 has not been proved. The defendant No. 1 also failed to prove the oral gift by the evidence of DW 5 who deposed that he did not see the mother of defendant No. 1, Nur Rahman, and thus the factum of oral gift dated 15-12-1973 has not been proved. Both the Courts below also concurrently found that the oral gift dated 15-12-1973 has not been proved. Since the possession of the defendant No. 1 has been proved for more than 12 years, the defendant No. 1 is entitled to get title even on the basis of invalid title, though the defendant No.1 did not specifically claim title by adverse possession vide the decision reported in 7 DLR 94.</u>

<u>31. It is an established principle of law that the revisional Court does not interfere in the concurrent finding of fact save in exceptional circumstances. The decision of our apex Court has set limit of the revisional power. Our Appellate Division in the case of Santosh Kumar Chakraborty vs MA Motaleb Hossain reported in 36 DLR (AD) 248 held that the High Court Division under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure only can interfere in the concurrent finding of the Courts below where it is found glaring misconception of law and non-consideration of material evidence.</u>

32. Revisional jurisdiction under section 115 is meant primarily for correcting errors made by Sub-ordinate Courts in the exercise of their jurisdiction and not those which are made in their discretion, unless the discretion is exercised fancifully or arbitrarily.

33. High Court in revision cannot interfere with the decision of the Subordinate Court unless it has exercised a jurisdiction not conferred by law or has failed to exercise jurisdiction so conferred upon it or has acted illegally in the exercise of jurisdiction which means that it has committed a breach of some provisions of law or with material irregularity in the exercise of its jurisdiction which means that it has committed some error of recorder during the course of trial and this breach or error has affected its ultimate exercise of jurisdiction. The order of the subordinate Court whether right or wrong shall be final unless such decision can be brought within the three conditions provided in section 115.

34. Where the trial Court passed the judgment and decree on proper appreciation of the evidence on record which have been affirmed by the appellate Court and the revisional Court on perusing the same refused to interfere with it. As the judgment and decree do Dot suffer from any legal infirmity, the Appellate Division also declined to interfere.

35. We received support of the above view in the case of Government of Bangladesh represented by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Rev) Perojpur; vs Abdul Hoque Khan and others 3 MLR (AD) 255.

36. Unless there is a case of misreading or non-consideration of material evidence on record resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice, the revisional Court cannot interfere with concurrent finding of facts of the trial Court as well as the appellate Court.

37. As the first two Courts concurrently found that the plaintiff has miserably failed to prove her allegation as to falsity of the unregistered deed of gift dated 19-6-1948 and the defendant No.1, on the other hand, has proved its genuineness, as such, concurrent findings of the Courts below cannot be interfered. Moreover, the learned Courts below have concurrently found the possession of the defendant No. 1 in 'Ka' and 'kha' schedule land on the basis of unregistered deed of gift dated 19-6-1948. On scrutiny of the evidence; we have also found that there is no misreading and non reading of material evidence on record or misconstruction of any documents in the findings of the Courts below. The findings of the Courts below are not perverse and contrary to Jawor evidence resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

38. The impugned judgment and decree passed by the appellate Court are well reasoned backed by sufficient oral and documentary evidence and all issues involved in the suit have rightly been settled, considered and decided by the trial Court as well as by the appellate Court with reference to the evidence and materials on record, which cannot be interfered.

39. Having considered the facts and circumstances of the case and foregoing narrative, we are led to the conclusion that the impugned judgment and decree do not suffer from any illegality and impropriety which call for no interference by this Court. Thus, the revision having no merit fails.

40. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and decree dated 5-11-2003 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Court No.2, Rangpur, in other Appeal No. 5 of 2003 dismissing the appeal and affirming those of the judgment and decree dated 24-9-2002 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, Court No.1, Rangpur in Other Suit No. 30 of 1997 decreeing the suit in part is affirmed.

Send down the LCR at once.

End.
