full_judgment:
Syed Amirul Islam, J: This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties in following terms:

"Let a Rule be issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why a contempt proceeding should not be drawn up against them for willful disobedience in handing over the delivery of the machinery despite order of stay granted by this Court on 5-11-97 passed in Writ Petition No. 3285 of 1996 or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper."

2. The short facts relevant for the purpose of disposal of the Rule are that, the petitioner company took loan from Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sangstha (Hereinafter called "the BSRS ") for establishment of its factory for which a loan was granted and an amount to Taka 51.89 lakh were given till 3-12-86. The petitioner company also took a loan from the Agrani Bank, Abdul Hamid Branch, Pabna and on its failure to repay the loan amount the Agrani Bank instituted Money Suit No. 14 of 1996 against the petitioner company for recovering a sum of Taka 27,31,236.15/- and in that Money Suit the BSRS was impleaded as proforma respondents No. 3. In that suit the Agrani Bank filed an application for attachment of the project properties before judgment which was allowed and against that order of attachment the petitioner company filed Writ Petition No. 3285 of 1996 wherein the impugned orders dated 18-4-1996 and 21-4-1996 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat was stayed till disposal of the Rule and the Division Bench also directed the respondents to unlock and hand over the possession of the Mill to the petitioner company immediately and further proceedings of the aforesaid Money Suit was stayed till disposal of the said writ petition.

3. It appears that at no point of time the factory was under lock and key pursuant to the order passed by the Artha Rin Adalat but nevertheless by order No. 23 dated 19-6-87, the Artha Rin Adalat, Pabna directed the Nazir of the Court to unlock the Mill concerned and hand over the possession of the same to the present petitioner but since it was never under lock and key the petitioner was directed to run the Mill. It further appears that the BSRS by a notice under reference No. 17.03.09.05/6943 dated 12-10-92 under Article 34 of the BSRS Order, 1972 and the BSRS (Direct Sale of Mortgaged Property) Rules, 1981 asked the petitioner company and its directors to pay company's loan liabilities amounting to Taka 1,70,26,000/- as on 31-7-92 but the company and its directors did not pay any money, whereupon on 13-4-96 BSRS advertised in the daily Inqilab a Public Notice for sale of the first mortgaged properties of the Company. Against that public notice the petitioner company as plaintiff filed Title Suit No. 2 of 1996 in the 2nd Commercial Court, Dhaka, challenging the validity and propriety of the Public Notice for sale of the said mortgaged properties. In that suit the BSRS filed an application under Order VII rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the plaint of the aforesaid Title Suit No.2 of 1996 and the learned Court after hearing the parties by its order dated 29-7-1999 rejected the plaint of the aforesaid Title Suit and that order has been accepted by the company and they did not challenge the propriety of that order by preferring any appeal before the High Court Division. After the rejection of that plaint and since there was no injunction order issued by this Court in the Writ Petition, the BSRS sold the machineries of the plant to one Mr Wares Zaman of Balu Bari, Dinajpur for a consideration of Taka 6 lakh by a public auction which was participated by three tenderers of which the said Zaman was the highest bidder. It appears that BSRS also instituted Miscellaneous Case No. 588 of 1998 in the Court of District Judge, Dhaka for recovery of Taka 432.33 lakh on 1-7-98 and the same was duly decreed against the present petitioner and its directors. The learned District Judge decreed realisation of Taka 4,32,33,000/- from the opposite parties as was due on 1-7-98 with interest at the rate of 16% per annum till realisation of the amount. Against the aforesaid decree the present petitioner company and its directors filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 145 of 2000 before the High Court Division. But in that Miscellaneous Appeal a Division Bench of this Court did not pass any order of status quo or any other prohibitory order. It appears that on 28-1-2001 a Division Bench of the High Court Division heard an application for maintaining the status quo in respect of the machineries involved in the case till the disposal of the appeal in Civil Rule No. 4 7 (FM) of 2001d and the BSRS was asked to show cause why the order of status quo in respect of the concerned machineries should not be granted. During the pendency of that proceeding the present petitioner company filed contempt petition No. 99 of 1997 against the Subordinate Judge and the Branch Manager, Agrani Bank, Pabna and accordingly, Rule was issued upon them. But BSRS was not a party in the aforesaid Contempt Petition No. 99 of 1997 subsequently, the BSRS Board in its 226th meeting held on 27-12-1998 decided to sell the machineries of the plant to the highest tenderer at a price of 6 lakh (as-it-is where it-is-basis) and pursuant to the decision of the Board BSRS issued Sale Certificate under rule 9 of the (Direct Sale of Mortgaged Property) Rules 1981 as the rule requires the BSRS to issue a sale certificate when the full sale price of the mortgaged property has been deposited under rule 8. In this state of affairs on 30-11-2000 BSRS sought for legal opinion from its adviser Mr AKM Nazrul Islam, Barrister-at-Law, Senior Advocate of the Supreme Court to give his valued opinion as to whether during the pendency of so many cases including contempt and writ petition relating to the company, it is advisable to hand over the machineries of the company to the buyer. The legal adviser i.e. the present opposite party No. 3 gave his opinion to the effect that BSRS should deliver the machinery to the buyer as soon as possible. He further opined that Article 34 proceeding regarding the sale and transfer of the project land and building, etc. should be kept in abeyance for some time and in the meantime, steps should be taken for hearing of the pending matters in the High Court Division. It appears that the present opposite party Nos. 1-2 relying on the aforesaid legal opinion have, in due course, handed over the machineries to the highest bidder against which the petitioner filed the present contempt case. It is alleged by the petitioner that by handing over the machineries to the highest bidder the present opposite parties have committed contempt of this Court by violating the order dated 5-11-97 passed by the Division Bench in Writ Petition No. 3285 of 1996 whereby this Court stayed the operation of the orders dated 18-4-96 and 21-4-96 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, Pabna and stayed all further proceedings of Money Suit No. 14 of 1996 pending before him and also directed the respondents to remove the lock .and hand over the possession of the Mill concerned to the petitioner immediately and the petitioner will be allowed to run the mill as before.

4. Mr Ozair Farooque, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits present opposite parties have committed contempt of Court by handing over the machineries of the factory of the petitioner company to the buyer in violation of this Court's order dated 5-11-96 passed in Writ Petition No. 3285 of 1996 whereby the orders dated 18-4-96 and 21-4-96 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge i.e. the respondent No.1 of the aforesaid writ petition, was stayed. It is further submitted that the opposite parties not only have willfully and intentionally violated this court's order but to frustrate the order of stay the BSRS have not granted further loan to the petitioner to run the factory.

5. Mr AKM Nazrul Islam, the learned Advocate appeared for the opposite party Nos. 1 & 2 as well as on his own behalf opposite party No. 3 and Mr Abdullah Al-Mamun, the learned Advocate also appeared on behalf of opposite party Nos. 1 and 2.

6. Mr Nazrul Islam, the learned Advocate advanced argument in extensoon the merits of the Rule. The learned Advocate drawing our attention to the order dated 5-11-96 passed in writ petition No. 3285 of 1996 submitted that in the aforesaid writ petition the BSRS was impleaded as proforma respondent No.3, and so also is the case in Money Suit No. 14 of 1996 wherein the respondent No.2 of the said Writ Petition namely, the Agrani Bank, was plaintiff and since the BSRS had the first charge on the property and Agrani Bank has the 2nd charge they impleaded BSRS as proforma respondent, their claim was against the petitioner for nonpayment of their dues. In that Money Suit, the respondent No.1 of the writ petition passed two orders namely, order dated 18-4-96 and 21-4-96 and by the first order the present petitioner was asked to show cause within 7 days why the property of the petitioner shall not be attached and by ad interim order of attachment the defendant Nos. 2 and 3 were restrained from interfering with the aforesaid property and by order dated 21-4-96 the Nazir of the court was directed to make an inventory of the machineries and thereafter to put it under lock and key under Order XXXIX rule 7 of the Code of Civil Procedure but the learned Subordinate Judge, Pabna by his order No. 23 dated 19-6-97 ultimately passed an order staying further proceedings of the aforesaid suit and directed the petitioner company to run the mill as it was not put under lock and key pursuant to the earlier order. Therefore, Mr Nazrul Islam submits that, in fact, the factory of the petitioner was never taken over either by the respondent No.1 or respondent No.2 of the writ petition in connection with the aforesaid money suit and BSRS, had nothing to do 'with the order as they were simply the proforma respondent and they did not take any steps ever to lock the factory of the petitioner. The learned Advocate then submits that the BSRS was also added in the writ petition as respondent and the stay order which was issued by this Court on 5-11-96 was, in fact, upon the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 of the aforesaid writ petition and it was not directed against the BSRS as they had nothing to do with the aforesaid order. The learned Advocate further submits that he as legal adviser rightly tendered his legal opinion stating that the BSRS is legally obliged to hand over the machineries to the highest bidder inasmuch as the BSRS is authorised by Article 34 of the BSRS Order as well as by rule 8 of the (Direct Sale of Mortgaged Property) Rule 1981 and more so when no injunction order was passed by this .Court restraining the BSRS in disposing of the machineries of the petitioners under the aforesaid Article and Rules and it is now well settled that the remedy provided by this Article 34 is an independent and alternative remedy available to the BSRS and against the decree granted by the District Judge under that Article 34 of BSRS order an appeal has been filed by the petitioner before the Court wherein no stay order has been passed nor the petitioner company preferred any appeal against the direct sale order issued by the BSRS in respect of the machineries in question. The learned Advocate therefore, most empathically submits that this Contempt petition is absolutely misconceived and unwarranted by the facts and circumstances of the case. The learned Advocate further submits that in the meantime writ petition itself has been disposed of by this Court and from the judgment it appears that the factory was handed over to the petitioner by the respondent No.1 of the aforesaid writ petition during the pendency of the writ petition pursuant to the order of this court. The learned Advocate referring to the order No. 23 dated 19-6-97 of the Money Suit submits that it is also found from that order that although there was an order of attachment before the judgment and also a direction was issued by the Court to put the factory under lock and key after making inventory but in fact, that order was never acted upon and the order dated 5-11-96 passed by this Court in the Writ Petition was duly complied with by the respondent No.1. Therefore, he contends that at no point of time neither the present opposite parties nor the other respondents of the aforesaid writ petition violated this court's order passed in the said writ petition.

7. Since an important question as to the liability of a lawyer in respect of giving legal opinion is involved in this case, we requested Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned former Attorney- General of Bangladesh, to assist us as amicus curiae.

8. Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned amicus curiae appeared before us on 3-7-02 and made his submissions. He submitted that from a perusal of the order dated 5-11-96 it appears that, in fact, the order of stay and direction given by this Court is against the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 of the said writ petition and BSRS had, in fact, nothing to do in the matter but nevertheless since the Court passed an order against all the respondents it would have been proper for the respondent No. 3 to seek a clarification from this court before giving the legal opinion. The learned Advocate then submits that it is now well settled that when an Advocate argues a case before the Court he is under the legal obligation to assist the Court properly and make a correct submission even if it goes against his client and for that no action can be brought against him by the client because of the fact that as an officer of the Court the Advocate owes a duty to the Court to tell the truth. Therefore, if an Advocate in a proceeding does something before the Court and his submission goes against the interest of his client he cannot be liable in negligence for such act/acts, he submits, Mr Mahmudul Islam further submits that the legal position is different so far it relates to his chamber work and an Advocate can be found guilty of negligence if he is found to be so in rendering legal advice. Mr Islam then submits that in this case although the respondent No.3 did not seek any clarification from the Court as to the true import of the order dated 5-11-96 but nevertheless he cannot be found to be negligent in tendering the legal opinion in question inasmuch as it reflected the correct legal position and he correctly assessed the legal position. Mr Islam finally submits that since the legal opinion tendered by the learned Advocate of BSRS is perfectly all right he cannot be held to be negligent in any way merely because he omitted to seek a clarification from this Court.

9. Mr Ozair Farooque, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, on the other hand, submits that from Annexure-'D' to the petition it is clear that the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 acted on the advice of their legal adviser and relying on the opinion the machineries were handed over to the highest bidder as a result of which the petitioner had to close down his business and therefore the legal opinion of the respondent No. 3 is responsible for prompting the other respondents to violate this Court order. If the learned Advocate is found negligent in discharging his professional duty surely he is guilty of negligence, the learned Advocate finally contends.

10. The learned Advocate Mr Nazrul Islam appeared in person and submitted that he tendered hundred percent correct opinions which are backed by a host of decisions of the Appellate Division. Mr Islam then submits that in the facts and circumstances of the case it was clear that although the direction was on the entire respondent to remove the lock and hand over possession of the mill to the petitioner, yet the BSRS had nothing to do in that respect inasmuch as they did not lock up the mill. Therefore, he contends that it was not necessary to seek any clarification from this Court more so when BSRS was impleaded as proforma respondent No.3. He further submits that from the materials on record it is clear that much earlier the factory of the petitioner was closed down and it is clear from order No. 23 dated 19-6-97 passed in Money Suit No. 14 of 1996 that the mill was never locked either by the Artha Rin Adalat or by the Agrani Bank in connection with the aforesaid Money Suit. Mr Nazrul Islam further submits that it is now well settled that Article 34 of the BSRS order is an independent, substantive and alternative mode of recovery of BSRS's dues and loans and therefore the sale of machineries cannot be said to be violative of the order dated 5-11-97 passed in Writ Petition No. 3285 of 96 more so when BSRS instituted Miscellaneous Case No. 588 of 1998 in the Court of District Judge, Dhaka for recovery of loan and the aforesaid case was decreed against the Company and against which the Company filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 145 of 2000 before this Court but there is no order of status quo or any other prohibitory order. Mr Nazrul Islam finally, submits that knowing fully well that he has not committed any contempt of this Court, the petitioner with malafide intention dragged him to his Court with a view to harass and humiliate him and therefore, an exemplary cost should be awarded against the petitioner to compensate his professional loss.

11. Mr. Abdullah-Al-Mammon, the learned Advocate also represented the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 and he also adopted the argument advanced by Mr. Nazra Islam. The learned Advocate finally submits that the respondent Nos. 1 and 2 honestly and sincerely acted upon the legal advice of the respondent No. 3 and thereby they have not committed any contempt of this Court.

12. We have perused the application along with the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the opposite parties and also gone through the Annexures. It appears that the petitioner has filed the present contempt petition against the opposite parties on the allegation that by delivering the machineries of the petitioner company to the buyer they have violated the Court's order dated 5-11-96 passed in Writ Petition No. 3285 of 1996. This writ petition arose out of Money Suit No. 14 of 1996 which was pending before the learned Subordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, Pabna, wherein the aforesaid Money Suit was instituted by the respondent No. 2 of the writ pennon as plaintiff against the petitioner of the writ petition and respondent No.3 of the writ petition was a proforma respondent in the Money Suit and during the pendency of that Money Suit an ad-interim order of attachment before judgment and direction to lock up the factory was passed by the Artha Rin Adalat. Against these orders the present petitioner moved this Court and obtained the Rule in the aforesaid writ petition wherein subsequently an application was filed by the petitioner with a prayer for stay of the impugned orders and also of stay of all further proceedings of Money Suit No. 14 of 1996 pending in the Artha Rin Adalat, Pabna and accordingly, the order dated 5-11-96 was passed whereby all further proceedings of Money Suit No. 14 of 1996 was stayed and the respondents were directed to unlock the factory and hand over the same to the petitioner. The admitted position is that the factory in question was never locked up by the respondent No.1 of the said writ petition. Moreover, it further appears from the judgment of the writ petition that the order dated 5-11-96 passed in the aforesaid writ petition was complied with by the respondent Nos. 1 and 2. Be that as it may, the present petitioner impleaded the BSRS as respondent No. 3 in the aforesaid writ petition, in spite of the fact that in the Money Suit the BSRS was impleaded as proforma defendant.

13. We have gone through the judgment passed by this Court in Writ Petition No. 3285 of 1996 on 28-11-2001 whereby this Courts order dated 5-11-96 so far it relates to order dated 21-4- 96 passed by the Artha Rin Adalat was made absolute as the learned trial Court vide order dated 19-6-97 complied with the order of this Court dated 5-11-96. Besides, the respondents in their affidavit-in-opposition have quoted the order No. 23 dated 19-6-97 from which it appears that at no point of time the mill was put under lock and key and the petitioner was directed to run the mill. In view of the materials on record it appears that the order dated 5-11-96 passed by this Court in the aforesaid writ petition has never been violated by anyone including the present respondents. Further, it appears that the instant contempt petition is absolutely misconceived and the averments made are baseless and contrary to facts. It appears that although the word respondents has been used in the order dated 5-11-96 but, in fact, it was directed against respondent Nos. 1 and 2 of the Writ Petition and not against BSRS because they were in no way connected with the orders dated 21-4-96 and 18-4-96 of the Money Suit No. 14 of 1996. It is also admitted that the terms of the order dated 5- 11-96 has duly been complied with by respondent No.1 during the pendency of the aforesaid writ petition. So, the allegation that the present opposite parties have violated the aforesaid order has no legs to stand on.

14. We have carefully examined the terms of the legal advice tendered by Mr Nazrul Islam, the legal adviser of the BSRS who is opposite party No.3 in this matter, and perused the provisions of BSRS Order along with the Direct Sale Rule. It appears that the legal adviser of the BSRS has in fact, tendered a correct' legal advice and the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 did not commit any illegality in handing over the possession of the machineries to the buyer and by doing that they have not violated the order dated 5-11-96 passed in the aforesaid writ petition. On a perusal of the materials on record it appears that the present Contempt Petition is absolutely misconceived and is a still born one. Here it may be mentioned that earlier on the selfsame allegation contempt petition No. 99 of 1997 was filed by the petitioner against the Artha Rin Adalat and Agrani Bank and not BSRS. Long thereafter the petitioner filed the present case against the BSRS including their legal adviser giving a go-by to their earlier case. From the averments of the contempt petition it is clear and admitted that the BSRS has filed Miscellaneous Case No. 588 of 1998 in the Court of District Judge, Dhaka for recovery of loan and that miscellaneous case was decreed against the present petitioner and its directors. However, the company and its directors filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 145 of 2000 before this Court which is still pending and there is no stay of the decree nor any direction was issued upon the BSRS to maintain status quo in respect of the concerned machineries. The further admitted position is that the BSRS has first charge on the assets of the petitioner Company and in order to raise working capital from Agrani Bank the BSRS allowed the petitioner Company to raise the same by creating a second charge on the assets. In due course the petitioner Company defaulted in repaying the loans of both the Banks and as a' result the aforesaid Miscellaneous case was filed by the BSRS and to realise their dues the Agrani Bank instituted Money Suit No.14 of 1996 before the Artha Rin Adalat. In this money Suit the BSRS was impleaded as proforma defendant whereas the petitioner Company and its directors were made principal defendants. In this Money Suit plaintiff Agrani Bank on 18-4-96 filed an application under Order XXXVIII rules 1-5 of the Code of Civil Procedure when a show cause was issued upon the present petitioner and they were also restrained by an order of ad-interim attachment not to transfer the properties to anyone in the meantime. Subsequently, on 21-4-96 the Agrani Bank filed an application under Order XXXIX rule 7 of the Code and prayed for making an inventory of the stores and machineries and then to lock it up and keep it under the control of the Court. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid orders the petitioner company filed Writ Petition No. 3288 of 96 and on 5-11-96 obtained an order of stay in respect of the aforesaid two orders dated 18-4-96 and 21-4-96 and all further proceedings of the Money Suit No. 14 of96 was also stayed. The respondents were also directed to remove the lock and hand over possession of the mill to the petitioner immediately. It appears from the judgment of the aforesaid Writ Petition that the said order was duly complied with by the learned Artha Rin Adalat. It further appears from Order No. 23 dated 19-6-96 that not only the order dated 5-11-96 was complied with but, in fact, the order dated 21-4-96 was never acted upon. In these backgrounds when decree of Miscellaneous Case No. 588 of 1998 was challenged before this Court, the BSRS in their attempt to realise some portion of the dues decided to sell the machineries of the petitioner Company when admittedly the mill was not in a running condition and resorted to article 34 of the BSRS Order and BSRS (Direct Sale of Mortgage Property) Rules 1981 and after complying with all the formalities sold the machineries to the highest bidder.

15. Here it may be mentioned that the BSRS by a notice under reference No. 17.03.09.05/6943 dated 12-10-92 issued under Article 34 of BSRS Order, 1972 and the BSRS (Direct Sale of Mortgaged Property) Rules, 1981 asked the petitioner Company and its directors to pay company's loan liabilities amounting to Taka 1,70,26,000/- as on 31-7-1992. But the petitioner Company and its directors did not pay any money and therefore on 13-4-96 BSRS had advertised in the "Daily lnqilab" a public notice for selling the first mortgaged properties. Against the aforesaid public notice the petitioner Company filed Title Suit No.2 of 1996 in the 2nd Commercial Court, Dhaka, challenging the aforesaid Public Notice. In that suit BSRS filed an application under Order VII rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the plaint and after hearing the parties the learned Court by its order dated 29-7-96 rejected the plaint against which the petitioner Company did not move the superior Court. Meanwhile, the machineries were sold on 16-2-99 as per BSRS Board decision dated 27-12-98. Then the Managing Director of the petitioner submitted an application dated 7-9-99 to deliver the machinery to him other than the purchaser at the same price but BSRS could not comply with his request since the sale procedure under Article 34 of BSRS Order, 1972 was concluded and sale certificate was issued to the buyer under Rule 9 of BSRS (Direct Sale of Mortgaged Property) Rules, 1981. In these backdrops the petitioner filed this contempt petition against the present respondents leaving aside the Artha Rin Adalat and the Agrani Bank. It is clear from the materials on record that Money Suit No. 14 of 1996 was instituted by the Agrani Bank and BSRS was not connected with that at all. Since BSRS holds the first charge on the property of the Petitioner Company their presence in the suit was necessary and, as such, they were impleaded as proforma defendant. BSRS had nothing to do with the order dated 5-11- 96 passed in Writ Petition No. 3285 of 1996. Admittedly, the Writ Petition was filed challenging the orders dated 18,4,96 and 21,4,96 passed by the Artha Rin Adalat and the order dated 5-11-96 was complied with by the learned Artha Rin Adalat with which BSRS was not concerned at all and no prohibitory order was passed against BSRS with regard to the sale of the machineries, Here it must be remembered that the sale proceeding was actually initiated in 1996 and that was not the subject matter of Money Suit No. 14 of 96. The application dated 9-7-99 of the Managing Director of the Petitioner Company also proves that there was no injunction or any other prohibitory order against BSRS. From the averments of the Contempt Petition it appears that the Petitioner Company has filed this case on false allegation only with the ill motive of harassing and humiliating the high officials of BSRS including its lawyer. The instant case is nothing but a vexatious litigation and the petitioner filed the case to exert pressure upon BSRS as they resorted to Article 34 of BSRS Order and (Direct Sale of Mortgaged Property) Rules. Therefore, we find and hold that the respondents have not committed any contempt of this Court in any way, more so when this Court itself in the aforesaid Writ Petition found that the order dated 5-11-96 has been complied with by the learned Artha Rin Adalat.

<u>16. Since we have found that the respondents have not in any manner violated this court's order date 5-11-96 we could dispose of the matter here. But in this case an important question as to the liability of an advocate has been raised. Therefore, we would like to address over-selves to that 'legal aspect. It has been settled for a century in England that a Barrister cannot be sued by his client for breach of contract because the fees he receives are an honorarium and there is no contractual relationship between a barrister and a client. This position continued until Hedley Byrne was decided by the House of Lords (1964) AC 465. In 1963a unanimous House of Lords held that in principle there was no difference between physical loss and financial loss and that a duty to take care in making statements existed whenever there was a special relationship and there had not been a disclaimer of responsibility. The said point was also emphasizedin Rooks vs Barnard (1964) A C 1129. Hedley Byrne affirmed and extended the principle that a duty to be careful as distinct from a duty to be honest may exist in situations other than those in which there is a contract between the parties. But there was doubt as to the Barrister's liability in negligence as a result of Hedley Byrne. These doubts were nearly all quietened when in Rondel vs Worsley(1969) AC 191, the House of Lords unanimously held that an Advocate could not be sued by his client in respect of alleged negligence in the conduct of a criminal trial. It should be remembered that Randel vs Worsleydoes not lay down the rule that a Barrister cannot be sued for negligence by his client. The case, in fact, lays down that as between Barrister and client there is a special relationship giving rise to a duty of care unless the Barrister can bring himself within the exceptional immunity of an Advocate. This immunity is quite distinct from the rule that there is no contractual relationship between the Barrister and client and is justifiable for a number of reasons on grounds of public policy because there is a general public interest in a free and independent Bar and a Barrister owes a duty to the Court for the hue administration of justice, or because an action for negligence against a barrister would inevitably involve the re-trial of the original proceeding or because the Barrister shares in general immunity which as given to all those taking part in the judicial process. But the law Lords in Saif Ali vs Mitchell and Co. (1980) AC 198, cut down the extent of immunity holding that a Barrister was liable when he carelessly failed to advise re-settling the plaintiffs claim so as to add another defendant. So, there might well be liability for an opinion given in chambers on point of law or for paperwork which was unconnected with litigation. But it by no means follows that there is a liability in negligence if an error takes place outside the area of immunity if a Barrister is careful in doing his professional works. So, in order to avoid liability outside the area of immunity a Barrister must be careful; he need not be right. Thus, on final analysis it comes to this that a lawyer is immune from an action in negligence so far his duty relates to actual advocacy in the Court or does something in connection with litigation. But so far it relates to giving legal opinion or doing other paperwork not connected with litigation, he is liable in negligence. He owes a duty of care to his client. So in discharging his professional duties as a lawyer he must be careful and must not be careless though not necessarily he must be right. However, a lawyer would not be liable for giving casual advice during a journey or in the course of informal conversation. A lawyer would, therefore, be liable for his work in chamber not connected with litigation. So, if a lawyer is found to be careless in rendering legal advice in the course of his professional duty, he would be liable in negligence.</u>

<u>17. This principle is said to be founded on the principle that a person who undertakes to do work which requires special skill holds himself out as having that skill; the lack of it then becomes blameworthy: imparitia culpa adnumeratur. It must be remembered that the obligation to exercise that skill does not depend on any contract or undertaking but based on the ground that of a reasonable man. As a necessary corollary the standard of care required is the degree of skill which is normally shown by a person doing that kind of work. The test is the standard of ordinary skilled man exercising and professing to have that special skill. A man need not possess the highest expert skill. It is well established law that it is sufficient if he exercises the ordinary skill of an ordinary competent man exercising that particular art. See (1957) 1 WLR 582 at 586. Lord Haldane LJ said in Nocton vs Ashburton(Lord), the solicitor contracts with his client to be skillful and careful. For failure to perform his obligation he may be made liable at law in contract or even in tort, for negligence in breach of a duty imposed on him" See (1914) AC 932 and (1953) Ch. 280. Nevertheless, it has repeatedly been held that the duty owed by a solicitor is a contractual duty owed to his client alone. See (1939) IKB194, (1953 CH 280 and (1958) 1 WLR 563. The question of his liability in tort would only arise when there is no contract. It must be borne in mind that what applies to a solicitor, applies to a lawyer in Bangladesh.</u>

<u>18. Besides, our statutory law also makes it clear that a lawyer may be reprimanded, suspended or removed from practice if he is found guilty of professional or other misconduct. See the Bangladesh Legal Practitioners and Bar Council Order, 1972 and the Rules framed there under. In Bangladesh an advocate can also be proceeded against for breach of contract if he is negligent in discharging his professional responsibilities. Therefore, the lawyers of this country are under the obligation to act reasonably and carefully in discharging their professional duties except so far it relates to actual advocacy in a Court of law otherwise he will be liable to his client either in negligence for breach of contract or in tort.</u>

19. In the present case we have found that the legal opinion tendered by Mr Nazrul Islam is in accordance with law and, in fact, there has been no contempt of this Court for violation of the order dated 5-11-96 and in spite of that the petitioner has initiated this proceedings impleading the high officials of the BSRS including their adviser and it appears to us that Mr Nazrul Islam has rightly submitted that this attempt on the part of the petitioner company is nothing but an attempt to unduly delay the payment of the BSRS dues and to. Delay the disposal of the pending legal proceedings in different Courts. It is a unique case wherein a Senior Advocate of this Court has been unnecessarily hackled by initiating this contempt proceeding and such unholy attempt must be nipped in the bud. Therefore, the petitioner should be saddled with a cautionary cost of Taka 25,000/- to be paid to respondent No. 3.

In view of our aforesaid discussions we do not find any substance in this Rule and accordingly, the Rule is discharged with a cost at Taka 25,000/- to be paid by the petitioner to the respondent No. 3 within 3(three) months from date.

End.

full_judgment:
Md Abdul Quddus J: This FA 337 of 2003 is preferred against judgment dated 25-3-2003 by Joint District Judge, 3rd Court Dhaka rejecting plaint of TS No. 194/2002 under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure and formal decree framed thereunder.

2. It is stated that Sonali Bank as plaintiff filed Civil Suit No. 254/2001 in the Court of Joint District Judge, and Artha Rin Adalat No.1 Dhaka against M Tariqullah Sikder as defendant for realisation of loan money from him with interest said suit was decreed ex parte on 18-4-2002 by Artha Rin Adalat No. 1 as above. M Tariqullah as plaintiff filed separately TS No. 194/2002 in the court of Joint District Judge 3rd Court Dhaka to set aside aforesaid ex parte Judgment and decree passed by Artha Rin Adalat No.1 in Artha Rin Suit No. 254 of 2002.

3. Sonali Bank as defendant appeared in TS No. 194/2002 and filed an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejecting the plaint of above suit being barred under section 6 of Artha Rin Adalat Act, 1990.

4. Court below after hearing both sides allowed application under Order VII, rule II, Code of Civil Procedure and rejected the plaint of TS 194 of 2002 vide judgment dated 25-3-2003.

5. Being aggrieved, the plaintiff of TS 194 of 2002 as appellant preferred this FA 337 of 2003. On prayer by appellant Civil Rule No. 705(F)/2003 was issued calling upon the opposite party to show cause as to why Artha Jari case 333/2003 of Joint District Judge & Artha Rin Adalat No.1 Dhaka should not be stayed till disposal of FA 337/2003. Rule was issued and it was made returnable within 2 weeks.

6. Learned Advocate for plaintiff-appellant frankly admits that Civil Suit No. 254 of 2001 was decreed ex parte on 18-4-2002 against Md Tariqullah Sikder as defendant in that suit. He submits that summons of the said Artha Rin Adalat case was fraudulently suppressed and the present appellant as defendant had no occasion to be aware of Civil Suit No. 254/2001 filed in Artha Rin Adalat which was decreed ex parte in the said suit. He submits that against such ex parte judgment and decree TS 194/2002 was rightly filed separately to set aside said ex parte decree. In such connection he refers to provision of section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure and also relies on a decision reported in 1996 BLD 423, 49 DLR 248 (Md Shahidullah vs Abdus Sobhan Talukder). He contends that the appeal must succeed.

7. Learned Advocate for respondent Sonali Bank in reply refers to the decision in the case of Sikdar Jute Bailing Ltd vs Sonali Bank reported in 1998 BLD (AD) 268 wherein it was held that separate suit to set aside ex parte decree passed by Artha Rin Adalat will not be maintainable in view of remedy available under Artha Rin Adalat Act itself.

8. Learned Advocate shows from Artha Rin Adalat Act 1990 that initially there was no provision and scope for filing Miscellaneous case under Order IX, rule 13, Code of Civil Procedure to set aside ex parte decree passed by Anha Rin Adalat, but subsequently through amendment provision was inserted for such relief under Order IX, rule 13, Code of Civil Procedure to set aside ex parte judgment and decree on deposit of 50% of decretal amount. He submits that in the face of above provision and scope under Artha Rin Adalat Act itself separate suit to set aside ex parte decree passed by Artha Rain Adalat will be barred under section 6 of Artha Rin Adalat Act, 1990. He argues that learned court below, in view of such bar under section 6 of Act 1990 as to filing of separate suit, rejected the plaint of TS 194 of 2002 under Order VII, rule II of the Code of Civil 'Procedure vide impugned Judgment which calls for interference by this Division. According to him, the appeal must be dismissed.

9. We have considered contentions of both sides. We have perused the impugned judgment dated 25-3-2003 and also the memo of appeal filed against the same. We have perused the decision reported in 1998 BLD (AD) 268 and also perused provisions of section 6 of Artha Rin Adalat Act, 1990. We have also seen the provision inserted through amendment as to filing of miscellaneous case under Order IX, rule 13, Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside ex parte decree passed by Artha Rin Adalat on depositing 50% of the decretal amount.

10. It is obvious that M Tariqullah Sikder filed TS 194 of 2002 intentionally to set aside ex parte decree passed against him on 18-4-2002 by Artha Rin Adalat Case No. 254 of 2001 by Artha Rin Adalat No.1, Dhaka in order to avoid deposit of 50% of decretal amount as required under provisions of Artha Rin Adalat Act by subsequent amendment of Act 1990.

<u>11. Provision of section 6 of Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 bars filing of separate suit to set aside ex parte decree passed by Artha Rin Adalat. Only available scope for setting aside ex parte decree passed by Artha Rin Adalat in Artha Rin case is to file miscellaneous case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure by deposit of 50% of decretal amount. It clearly appears that TS 194 of 2002 was filed separately to set aside ex parte decree of Artha Rin Adalat in order to avoid deposit of 50% of decretal amount and filing miscellaneous case under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure as has been made available under said Act of 1990.</u>

12. In the above connection, decision reported in 1998 BLD (AD) 268 has been appropriately cited from the Bank. In the above decision it has been held that separate suit to set aside ex parte decree passed by Artha Rin Adalat will not be maintainable in view of the remedy available under Artha Rin Adalat Act itself, Cited decision on behalf of appellant as reported in 1996 BLD 423 has no manner of application in this appeal.

13. In the above context, we see no merit in this appeal, which must fail. In the result, FA 337/2003 is dismissed on contest with cost to the contesting respondent. Impugned Judgment and formal decree dated 18-4-2002 and 25-4-2002 passed by the court below are affirmed. Civil Rule No. 705(F)/2003 be accordingly, discharged.

Copy be sent down.

End.

full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J : Plaintiff presented the appeal against the decree dated 9-7-2000 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Court No.3 at Dhaka in Title Suit No. 14 of 1991, which dismissed the suit.

2. On 21-1-91 the plaintiff instituted the suit against the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka and three others for declaration of title in the suit land with building thereon fully described in the schedule to the plaint and for further declaration that the entire proceeding in certificate case No. 17 of 1986 including order of attachment and auction sale of the General Certificate Office at Dhaka were all illegal, without jurisdiction, void and of no legal effect.

3. Plaint case, in short, is that one Dr Saifuddin Ahmed got a perpetual lease for 99 years of the suit land measuring about 33 decimals, more or less one bigha in the local measurement. He built a house thereon; and while was thus in possession died leaving behind one wife, four sons and three daughters.

4. After his death, his legal representatives instituted Title Suit No. 417 of 1983 in the First Court of Munsif at Dhaka for partition and on amicable partition the suit property fell in the share of Anisuddin Ahmed, proforma defendant No.4 and husband of the plaintiff. Anisuddin Ahmed, thus became owner in possession of the suit property.

5. On 2-1-85 said Anisuddin Ahmed orally gifted the suit property to the plaintiff in front of other co-sharers and relations divesting himself of all his interest therein. Then, on 16-1-85 said Anisuddin Ahmed had sworn an affidavit before a Notary Public Mr Zahirul Hoque Khan, which was duly notarised.

6. Anisuddin Ahmed was then on 21-10-85 convicted by Special Martial Law Court No 7 under sections 406/420 of the Penal Code in Dhanmondi PS Case No. 12(8)84 and sentenced to suffer four years rigorous imprisonment and to pay fine of Taka 18,02,500 in default to suffer one year's rigorous imprisonment more. Then, the Chairman of the Martial Law Court asked the defendant No.1, Deputy Commissioner to realise the fine as a public demand under the Public Demand Recovery Act 1913 (Act III of 1913). Review by the Chief Martial Law Administrator was rejected by order dated 12-5-86.

7. While said pro-forma defendant No.4 was in custody undergoing sentence, defendant No. 2 asked defendant No.3, General Certificate Officer, Dhaka to commence a certificate proceeding. Accordingly, Certificate Case No. 17 of 1986 was started without however, any service of statuary notice upon said defendant No.4, the suit property was attached and then, placed for auction sale.

8. On 2-11-86, plaintiff made an objection to defendant No. 3 claiming that her husband Anisuddin Ahmed had no title or interest in the suit property. About one and half years before the certificate proceeding commenced, the plaintiff became lawful owner of the suit property. She also prayed for release of the suit property from the certificate proceeding. Thereupon and on the opinion of the government pleader the Certificate Officer by order dated 8-4-87 directed for inquiry and report as to whether any other property was owned and possessed by said certificate debtor excepting the suit property.

9. But on the prayer of the informant, Mizanur Rahman Chowdhury 16-9-87 was fixed for examination of the witnesses. The plaintiff presented three witnesses. In spite of proof furnished by the plaintiff that the suit property did not belong to said certificate debtor, Certificate Officer fixed 15-2-87 for auction sale of the suit property.

10. Then, the plaintiff unsuccessfully made appeals before the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), defendant No.2, the Additional Commissioner, Dhaka, the Land Appeal Board and the Secretary, Ministry of Land. Thus disappointed and frustrated, she was constrained to institute the suit.

11. By amendment of the plaint, she also stated that she got her name mutated by order dated 19-3- 92 both in the land record as well as in the Dhaka City Corporation.

12. Defendant No. 1 first alone then jointly with defendant Nos. 2 and 3 contested the suit by filing two written statements.

13. Their common case, in short, is that on 4- 8-84 one Mizanur Rahman lodged a FIR against Anisuddin and four others with Dhanmondi Police Station and Dhanmondi PS Case No. 12(8)84 was registered under sections 420 and 406 of the Penal Code. The case was then transferred to the Martial Law Court and registered as case 7 of 1985, By order dated 21-10-85 Anisuddin Ahmed along with others were convicted and sentenced to different periods and asked to pay Taka 35,00,000 with interest at the rate of 10% within six months. As the convicted persons failed to deposit the fine with interest within time the Deputy Commissioner asked for realisation of fine by attachment of the moveable and immovable properties of said convicted persons. As per order of the Martial Law Court, the General Certificate Officer started a case being No. 17 of 1986(fine) for realisation of Taka 18,02,500 from Anisuddin Ahmed. A notice under section 7 of Public Demand Recovery Act, 1913 was served upon the certificate debtor but he failed to file any written objection within time. Then, a notice under section 46 of the said Act was also served upon him. Then, Mrs Hasina Begum, wife of convicted Anisuddin Ahmed, claimed acquiring the suit property by way of oral gift. But she failed to prove the oral gift. Her appeal failed up to the Land Ministry. So, the plaintiff came up with false case of oral gift.

14. On the pleadings following issues were settled:

(a) whether the suit in the form and manner as framed was maintainable?

(b) was the suit barred by limitation?

(c) whether Anisuddin Ahmed gifted the suit property orally to the plaintiff and plaintiff had any title thereby?

(d) whether the certificate proceeding could be interfered with? and

(e) what relief the plaintiff was entitled to?

15. In support of her case, plaintiff examined four witnesses including herself while the defendant examined one witness, an assistant of the General Certificate Officer. The plaintiff also adjured number of papers, which were marked as exhibits 1 to 6 series while those of the defendants marked as Exhibit 'Ka' to 'Ja'.

16. On the evidence oral and documentary on record, learned Subordinate Judge found that on 20- 1-85 judgment was delivered by the Martial Law Court in Dhanmondi PS Case No. 12(8)84 under sections 420 and 406 of the Penal Code; that after the commencement of the case in 1984, the plaintiff claimed the suit property by way of an oral gift dated 2-1-85; that the plaintiff failed to prove oral gift beyond reasonable doubts; that the suit challenging such order of the certificate officer was hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act and that the plaintiff acquired no title in the suit land. Upon such view, learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit.

17. Whether the learned Subordinate Judge was justified in dismissing the suit on the evidence on record is the only issue facing us in this appeal.

18. Plaintiff's case, as stated above, is that father-in-law of the plaintiff, Dr Saifuddin Ahmed, got the suit property by way of perpetual lease for 99 years from the C&B Department by a registered deed of lease dated 4-5-56. On getting possession of the suit land, he made one-story building on the suit land. He died leaving one wife, four sorts and three daughters. After his death, in Partition Suit No. 417 of 1983 in the First Court of Munsif the suit property along with other property were amicably partitioned amongst said heirs and the suit property fell in the share of her husband, Anisuddin Ahmed.

19. Anisuddin Ahmed then orally gifted the suit property to the plaintiff on 2-1-85 in presence of other co-sharers and relations. Anisuddin also had sworn an affidavit before Mr Zahirul Haq Khan, Notary Public and an Advocate of the Supreme Court, who duly notarised the affidavit, Exhibit 1. After such gift the plaintiff Hasina Begum, wife of Anisuddin Ahmed, possessed the suit property as her own.

20. In support of her case, the plaintiff deposed as PW 1, particularly on oral, gift, in presence of witnesses.

21. PW 2 Mrs Helena Akhter, aged about 61 years, elder sister of the plaintiff, proved oral gift of the suit property to the plaintiff on 2-1-85. She retired as senior officer of Uttar a Bank. She said that at the time of oral gift, she was present along with PW 3 Moniruddin Ahmed, younger brother of Anisuddin Ahmed, Azizuddin Ahmed and PW 4 Abul Kalam Azad, neighbour.

22. PW 3, Moniruddin Ahammad, aged 57, former Chief Engineer of BADC and retired as such, younger brother of said Anisuddin Ahmed also corroborated the plaintiff that on 2-1-85 Anisuddin Ahmed gifted the suit property to the plaintiff in his presence and in presence of neighbour PW 4 Azad and PW 2 Selena Khan.

23. PW 4, Abul Kalam Azad, aged about 78, an Advocate of the Supreme Court, corroborated PW 1 that on 2-1-85 said Anisuddin Ahmed orally gifted the suit property to the plaintiff in presence of them.

24. Besides, an affidavit sworn by Anisuddin Ahmed on 16-1-85 and duly notarised was also produced and marked Exhibit 1.

25. Learned Subordinate Judge could not rely upon the evidence of said witnesses on the ground that they were closely related. In case of an oral gift by husband to his wife, it is natural for their relations to be present and not any stranger. PW 4 Abul Kalam Azad, an Advocate of the Supreme Court who is not a relation but a neighbour, was also present. Learned Subordinate Judge unnecessarily exercised his energy to entertain doubt on the oral gift. Such doubt on the evidence on record cannot be justified.

26. Secondly, learned Subordinate Judge missed the important point. Martial Law Court No. 7 by its order dated 21-10-85, Exhibit-'Kha', convicted Anisuddin Ahmed and four others under sections 420 and 406 of the Penal Code and sentenced Anisuddin Ahmed to suffer rigorous imprisonment for four years and to pay a fine of Taka 18,02,500 with interest at the rate of 10% within six months; in default, to suffer rigorous imprisonment for one more year.

27. Learned Subordinate Judge found that convict Anisuddin Ahmed has already suffered 4 + 1 = 5 years of sentence. After having suffered the sentence awarded in lieu of fine, if the certificate proceeding for realisation of the fine is allowed to continue then Anisuddin Ahmed would have to face double jeopardy. Article 35(2) of the Constitution prohibits punishment more than once for the same offence.

<u>28. Lastly, the learned Subordinate Judge along with all other functionaries of the state appear to have pursued the certificate proceeding like a catholic. They failed to understand the legal effect of an order particularly an executory order of the martial law authority after revocation of the Martial Law and restoration of the Constitution. It is now well settled by good authorities that after revocation of the martial law and restoration of the Constitution, all those orders that are executory in nature on the date of such revocation come to an end. Reason is very simple, all authority and force that demand execution are derived from the martial law proclamation and with the exit of the martial law proclamation, such orders pending for execution on the date of revocation of the martial law loses all their efficacy and force. After restoration of the Constitution no order of the martial law authority therefore could be expected to be executed under the Constitution or by any constitutional authority. It must be remembered that Martial Law is a slur on the Constitution.</u>

<u>29. Appellate Division in Nasrin Kader Siddique vs Bangladesh and others, 44 DLR (AD) 16 held that</u>

<u>"Therefore, the proclamation of martial law, martial law offences and martial law courts die a natural death when the martial law is revoked ... "</u>

30. In view of above legal position, entire certificate proceeding arising out of certificate case No. 17 of 1986 including all orders passed therein are coram non judice and without jurisdiction; and therefore, liable to be quashed.

31. The plaintiff having proved to have acquired good title in the suit property by way of gift has got every right to protect such property. The view of the learned Subordinate Judge that the suit for declaration of title on the basis of oral gift is barred by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act is therefore, wholly based on misconception of law.

32. In the circumstances, impugned judgment and decree cannot be sustained in law. Appeal therefore, succeeds.

33. In the result, the appeal is allowed without however any order as to cost. Impugned judgment and' decree are hereby set aside. The suit of the plaintiff is decreed; title of the plaintiff in the suit property is accordingly declared and entire certificate proceeding of Certificate Case No. 17 of 1986 including orders for attachment and auction sale is also declared without jurisdiction, illegal and void; and accordingly, quashed.

Send down the records at once.

End.
